# MetaML Workbench — Deep Technical Audit Report

**Repository:** `metaml-workbench-source-of-truth` → `https://github.com/nirmantaterh/metaml_su_2026.git`
**Branch:** `master` (clean, up to date with origin)
**Last commit:** `800beb8` — "chore: remove local Claude Code configuration"
**Audited:** all source, tests, docs, ADRs, demo fixtures, build configs

---

## 1. MetaML in One Paragraph

MetaML is a multi-semester NYU ITP research platform with a long-term vision of a **decentralized network for discovering, sharing, and reusing AI components** (bots, models, workflows) across peer-to-peer nodes. The intended ecosystem combines a taxonomy layer for classifying components, a business-context layer describing what components do, a metrics layer tracking performance, and a KMP event protocol (BSR/SUR/SUN/MUR message types) nodes use to negotiate and exchange components autonomously. The full picture spans multiple sub-teams and semesters. The "complete" platform — including the actual P2P DHT routing network built by a Fall 2025 team (Jason Choi, Yuwen Zhong in codebase `p2p_fall25`) — is **separate** from this repository and was not touched this semester.

---

## 2. Our Semester Contribution

**Team 3** (Emily Chen, Henry Weisman, Nirman Taterh, Summer 2026) owns **Task 1** fully and pieces of Tasks 2 and 3 from the MetaML platform's own breakdown:

What Team 3 actually built in this repository:

- A **React + bpmn-js BPMN modeling tool** integrated with a Spring Boot + Camunda 7.22 backend
- **Code generation**: from a BPMN model → a complete standalone Spring Boot + Camunda application, written to disk and launched as a real child JVM
- **Digital Twin runtime**: auto-generation and deployment of a synchronized Twin process instance running inside the same Camunda engine as the Original, with `AFTER_COMMIT`-triggered synchronization
- **Two generation modes**: single-BPMN (Workbench-derived Twin) and two-BPMN authored (professor-supplied RedCollar Proxy/Twin with RabbitMQ lockstep synchronization via a generated `SignalBroadcaster`)
- **Node Manager client + stub server**: HTTP client to a static properties-file-backed agent catalog (our portion of Task 2 — client-side only)
- **Governance system** (full ownership of Task 3): platform-level quota (deny-list + per-twin evolution/execution budgets) and durable tenant-scoped policy engine (Tenant → Policy → Version → Rule → ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL) with an Approvals workflow
- A **regression test suite** of 299 tests including concurrency, multi-instance, failure-isolation, synchronization, and walkthrough tests
- **15 ADRs**, an Architecture Specification, an Evolution Timeline, and 7 runtime diagrams
- A formal **Phase 7 adversarial red-team review** (7-agent independent pass) followed by **Phase 7.5** empirical resolution of the 3 highest-priority findings

---

## 3. End-to-End Workbench Flow

**What the repository actually proves:**

```
1. Model (BPMN)
   User draws/imports BPMN in bpmn-js editor → "Save" deploys it to
   the embedded Camunda engine + records a ProcessModel in WorkbenchStateStore.
   Save creates a NEW model id every time — never overwrites.

2. Generate (Target Harness Platform)
   SpringBootProjectGenerator copies templates/camundademo, writes:
   - One Java delegate class per unique camunda:delegateExpression (DelegateClassGenerator)
   - One REST endpoint per externally-triggerable activity: USER_TASK, RECEIVE_TASK,
     EXTERNAL_TASK (BpmnActivities.Trigger classification)
   - The BPMN itself
   - A .metaml-project.properties file for stable process-key identity
   Collision detection: two delegate expressions mapping to the same Java class name →
   InvalidDelegateExpressionException naming the losing bpmnElementId → "Go to error" in UI.

3. Launch (child JVM)
   SpringBootProjectLauncher shells out: mvn clean install then mvn spring-boot:run.
   A free port is assigned dynamically (ServerSocket probe). Waits up to 5 min for
   a TCP probe to confirm readiness. Tracks running processes in ConcurrentHashMap.
   Generated apps use in-memory H2 (process-engine); Workbench uses file H2 (camunda).
   Generated-project registry rebuilt at startup from filesystem + WorkflowEventStore.

4. Twin (Workbench-internal digital twin)
   TwinModelGenerator.generate() transforms the Original's DEPLOYED BpmnModelInstance:
   - Every User Task → Receive Task (TwinAdvance_<id>) + Service Task (twinAutomationDelegate)
   - Multi-instance User Tasks wrapped in embedded sub-processes (sequential and parallel)
   - Gateways, plain end events copied as-is
   - Boundary events dropped; unsupported types fail with named diagnostics
   Deterministic: stabilized ids, stripped DI diagram, so relaunch reuses same deployment.
   Both Original and Twin start in the same launch call; rolled back atomically if Twin fails.
   Business keys: original-<twinId> / twin-<twinId>.

5. Synchronization (Original → Twin)
   AutoBridgeTrigger: @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) on Camunda's ExecutionEvent.
   Fires after Original commits an activity start. Dispatches on a single-thread ExecutorService
   ("auto-bridge"), blocks with 6s timeout so UI always sees result.
   bridgeActivityEvent():
     - Resolves linked Twin activity via ActivityLink (the one persisted cross-reference)
     - Checks alreadyEvolved guard (via HistoricDetail.variableUpdates() - restart-safe)
     - Calls NodeManagerClient to look up agent (→ nodemanager stub at :8083)
     - Writes evolvedAgent_* variables onto Twin instance
     - Correlates Twin's Receive Task (execution-targeted for parallel MI siblings)
     - TwinAutomationDelegate runs synchronously in same command → ProjectAutomationService
     - AgentExecutionDelegate copies Twin outputs back onto Original

6. Governance (before every evolution)
   Two independent layers in order:
   A) Platform quota (GovernanceServiceImpl, runtime-only):
      - Deny-list: agent types not permitted at all
      - Evolution budget: per-twin limit on agent requests (default 25, AtomicInteger)
      - Execution budget: per-twin limit on Twin token steps (default 200, AtomicInteger)
   B) Tenant policy (PolicyDecisionEngine, durable via TenantPolicyStore JSON):
      - Tenant → Policy → Active Version → Rules → ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL
      - Platform policies (tenantId==null) win on ties with tenant policies
      - REQUIRE_APPROVAL → ApprovalStore pending row → operator approve/reject → execute

7. RedCollar Target Platform (Demo 5 — generated app with RabbitMQ)
   A second generation mode: two authored BPMNs (Proxy + Twin authored separately)
   → SpringBootProjectGenerator.generateWithAuthoredTwin() using backend/RedCollarTP template
   → Generated platform embeds SignalBroadcaster: @Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000ms), polls
     Camunda's event-subscription state to detect "both sides waiting on same signal"
   → Activity handoff: Proxy waits → SignalBroadcaster publishes task to RabbitMQ queue
   → Twin worker executes → response published back → Proxy advances
   Note: this is a DIFFERENT mechanism from the Workbench's own AFTER_COMMIT bridge.
```

## 6. Original/Twin Mechanics

### What is the Original?
A real Camunda `ProcessInstance` started on the user's own deployed BPMN definition, with real user tasks a human works through via REST calls to the generated endpoints or directly. Business key: `original-<twinId>`.

### What is the Twin?
A second Camunda `ProcessInstance`, sharing the same engine and H2 datasource, started on a **separately generated BPMN** (`TwinModelGenerator.generate()`). Business key: `twin-<twinId>`. The Twin has no human-facing tasks — every User Task has been replaced by a Receive Task + Service Task pair.

### How the Twin BPMN is Generated
`TwinModelGenerator.generate()` walks the Original's *deployed* `BpmnModelInstance` breadth-first, applies transformation rules (User Task → Receive/Service pair; multi-instance → embedded sub-process wrapper; gateways/end events copied as-is; unsupported types → explicit exception). Output is deterministic: random Camunda-builder ids are stabilized via `stabilizeMessageIds`, `stabilizeMultiInstanceIds`, explicit id assignment; DI diagram is stripped. This determinism is load-bearing: `enableDuplicateFiltering(true)` reuses the same Twin deployment on relaunch instead of accumulating versions.

### Synchronization Mechanism
`AutoBridgeTrigger` — a `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true)` on Camunda's `ExecutionEvent` (republished by Camunda's Spring Boot Starter's `EventPublisherPlugin`). Fires after the Original commits each activity start. Runs bridge on a dedicated single-thread `ExecutorService` ("auto-bridge"). The listener blocks with a 6-second timeout so the calling UI's response always reflects the bridge outcome. A stuck bridge replaces the executor so other twins aren't blocked.

### What Synchronization Does
`bridgeActivityEvent(twinId, activityId, activityInstanceId)`:
1. Resolves the `ActivityLink` (the one persisted mapping: Original activity id ↔ Twin activity id)
2. `alreadyEvolved` guard — uses `HistoricDetail.variableUpdates()` (counts variable *sets*, not just current value) to distinguish visits in a loop-back. Restart-safe because it reads Camunda history, not app memory.
3. Calls `NodeManagerClient.checkAgentAvailability(agentType)` → stub at `:8083`
4. Writes `evolvedAgent_*` / `evolvedAgentOutput_*` variables onto the Twin instance
5. Resolves the correct Camunda `executionId` the Twin's Receive Task is waiting on (for parallel multi-instance: via `createEventSubscriptionQuery()` + non-local `loopCounter` read, disambiguated by `messageEventReceived(messageName, executionId)`)
6. Correlates the Receive Task, which immediately runs the synchronous Service Task (`TwinAutomationDelegate`) in the same Camunda command
7. `AgentExecutionDelegate` (a `camunda:taskListener event="complete"` on the Original's user task) copies the Twin's evolved agent and outputs back onto the Original

### Failure Semantics
If the synchronous automation throws, the entire Camunda command rolls back — both the Receive Task correlation and the Service Task — leaving the Twin's wait state intact and safe to retry. The failure becomes a Camunda Incident (`runtimeService.createIncident(...)`) visible in Cockpit. Incident-driven policy was chosen specifically because `ProjectAutomationService.execute()` has no idempotency contract; blanket retry could double-invoke external agents.

### What Has Been Empirically Validated
- `AFTER_COMMIT` necessity (plain `@EventListener` fires before flush, leaving "not yet reached" state — discovered empirically)
- Synchronous rollback semantics for a failed Service Task (probe: delegate throws, event-subscription survives, retry succeeds)
- Parallel multi-instance sibling disambiguation via `messageEventReceived` (tried `localVariableEquals` and `processInstanceVariableEquals` — both failed; found via `javap` inspection of actual jar)
- Non-local vs local `loopCounter` asymmetry between Twin and Original sides (proved with 3-sibling probe)
- `createIncident` requires leaf execution (not scope execution) — `BadUserRequestException` hit and fixed
- `HistoricDetail.variableUpdates()` returns one row per set (not collapsed current value) — verified via `ZzHistoricDetailProbeTest`
- Twin determinism (generate same input twice, diff byte-for-byte — stabilization proven to work)
- `AdHocSubProcess` genuinely absent from `camunda-bpmn-model` 7.22.0 — `javap`-confirmed

### Demo 5 / RedCollar: Different Mechanism
The generated Target Platform (RedCollar) is a **separate**, independently-running JVM. It has its own Camunda engine (in-memory H2). Proxy and Twin are two process instances inside that generated app. Synchronization there uses `SignalBroadcaster`: a `@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000ms)` bean that polls Camunda's event-subscription state to detect "both sides waiting on the same signal," then publishes a task to a per-activity RabbitMQ queue (exchange: `redcollar.<projectId>.exchange`), the Twin worker consumes and executes, the response is published back, the Proxy's external-task worker runs. This is **not** event-driven — it is **1-second polling**. Verified by hand on 2026-08-23 (7 activities round-tripped over RabbitMQ, 9/9 Twin workers executed, both instances completed).

---

## 7. Governance

Two independent, non-overlapping layers:

### Platform Governance (`GovernanceServiceImpl`) — RUNTIME ONLY
- **Deny-list** (`deniedAgentTypes`): set of agent type strings; normalized to lowercase. Checked before any `reserveEvolutionSlot` call.
- **Evolution budget** (`maxEvolutionsPerTwin`, default 25): `AtomicInteger` per twin id. Uses increment-then-rollback (not check-then-increment) to prevent race conditions. Counts external agent-catalog requests. Released on failure. Reset to zero on app restart — **intentional**, documented in code comment and in ADR-013 and `GovernanceServiceImplTest`.
- **Execution budget** (`maxTwinExecutionsPerTwin`, default 200): same mechanism. Counts every Twin token step (gateways included). Reset on restart.
- Runtime overrides via `GovernanceController`/`updatePolicy` — survive until restart only.

### Tenant Governance (`TenantPolicyService` + `PolicyDecisionEngine`) — DURABLE
- Persisted via `TenantPolicyStore` (atomic-write JSON file). Survives restart.
- Structure: Tenant → Policy → PolicyVersion (DRAFT/ACTIVE/RETIRED) → PolicyRule → PolicyEffect (ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL)
- Rules have: `field` (currently `"action"` or custom attributes), `operator` (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`), `value`, `effect`
- Evaluation: `PolicyDecisionEngine.evaluate(GovernanceRequest)` finds the best matching rule across all active versions of all policies for the tenant (plus platform policies with `tenantId==null`). Platform policies win on tied severity.
- Default behavior: no matching rule → `ALLOW` (silence never blocks)
- `REQUIRE_APPROVAL` → creates a pending `Approval` record in `ApprovalStore` → operator approves/rejects → approved decision executes the pinned action.

### Scope
- Evaluated in `WorkbenchServiceImpl.runEvolution()` before every agent assignment
- A Twin with `tenantId == null` skips tenant evaluation (deliberately ungoverned)
- No authentication: `tenantId` is caller-supplied, never verified

### Limitations (explicit)
- Platform quota resets on restart (by design)
- W3 (open): `runEvolution` can report `approved=true` after partial write (agent variable set, some output writes lost)
- W8 (open): governance counter maps grow unboundedly (keyed by twin id, never cleaned up)

---

## 8. Node Manager

**Three distinct things must not be confused:**

### 1. Workbench Node Manager Client (`NodeManagerClient.java`)
A Spring `@Component` in the `workbench` library module. Makes HTTP GET calls to `http://localhost:8083/api/v1/node-manager/agents/{agentType}` with 1s connect / 2s read timeouts (tight so a stuck call can't block the single-thread auto-bridge worker indefinitely). Validates agent type and output names. Strips outputs with non-camelCase names or non-scalar values. This is what the Workbench actually uses during bridge/evolution.

### 2. Local Stub Node Manager (`backend/nodemanager` module)
A separate Spring Boot application (port 8083). `NodeManagerServiceImpl` backs its catalog from `NodeManagerProperties` — a `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix="nodemanager")` YAML config binding (`Map<String, AgentConfig>`). Returns `available=true` + `agentName` if the type is registered, `available=false` otherwise. **Static catalog — no actual P2P discovery, no actual ML agent lookup.** 6 tests.

### 3. The Real MetaML P2P Node Manager
Lives in the `p2p_fall25` codebase (Jason Choi, Yuwen Zhong, Fall 2025). Involves Kademlia DHT, KMP protocol, taxonomy/metrics/BSM management. **Not integrated with this repository.** `NodeManagerClient` hardcodes `localhost:8083` — it can only talk to the local stub.

**What exists:** client → stub integration, demonstrating the call pattern end-to-end.
**What does not exist:** real agent catalog, real P2P lookup, MCP-compliant API (explicitly future work in PLATFORM_CONTEXT.md).

## 12. Technical Core

The central technical contribution of this semester is the **Digital Twin Runtime** — specifically the implemented and empirically validated synchronization mechanism between the Original and Twin process instances.

**Why this is the technical core:**
- It is the non-obvious, novel engineering that distinguishes this from "a BPMN tool" or "a code generator"
- The mechanism took 8 evolutionary stages to converge, each driven by empirical failure rather than design assumption
- The correct answer (`AFTER_COMMIT` listener → dedicated thread → execution-targeted messaging for parallel instances → Receive Task wait state for Job Executor isolation) was not predictable from Camunda's public documentation alone — it required `javap` inspection, probe tests, and three successive adversarial reviews to reach a version that actually holds under concurrency and restart
- Every other piece of the system (code generation, governance, Node Manager client) is either more conventional or more easily substituted; the twin synchronization is where the actual research claim lives
- The Workbench-level synchronization (AFTER_COMMIT, in-process) and the Target Platform synchronization (RabbitMQ + 1-second polling) are architecturally distinct mechanisms addressing the same problem at different scopes — both being implemented and demonstrated in one semester is the depth of the claim

**Supporting evidence in repository:**
- 15 ADRs documenting the decision path
- 8-stage Evolution Timeline with every wrong turn recorded
- 7 runtime diagrams
- Phase 7 independent adversarial review (7 agents)
- Phase 7.5: 3 highest-priority findings corrected, each through at least one independent re-review that found and required fixing a real defect in the first fix attempt

## 14. Unsafe Claims

Do NOT make these:

- ❌ "MetaML authenticates tenants" — no authentication anywhere; tenantId is caller-supplied
- ❌ "Every BPMN error is automatically pinpointed to a specific element" — only delegate class-name collision and delegate-file write failures carry a `bpmnElementId`
- ❌ "Importing a BPMN validates it" — import means bpmn-js loaded the XML; Camunda validation happens only at Save
- ❌ "The system is production-ready" — no auth, JSON whole-file persistence, single-JVM concurrency, no formal API contract
- ❌ "Event-driven synchronization" (unqualified) — the Workbench's in-process Original↔Twin bridge is event-driven (AFTER_COMMIT); the generated Target Platform's Proxy↔Twin is a 1-second polling coordinator. These are different mechanisms
- ❌ "The Node Manager integrates with the MetaML P2P network" — the client hardcodes `localhost:8083`; the stub is a static YAML catalog
- ❌ "All BPMN constructs are supported in the Twin" — only User Tasks, Exclusive/Parallel/Inclusive Gateways, plain End Events, and literal-cardinality Multi-Instance are fully supported; many others fail generation loudly or are boundary events (dropped)
- ❌ "Governance quotas persist across restarts" — platform quota (deny-list, budgets) is runtime-only by deliberate design; only tenant policy is durable
- ❌ "Agents make autonomous decisions" — "agents" are catalog lookups; the stub returns static configured values
- ❌ "The system was built by our team from scratch" — the workbench application existed in earlier form; we substantially rebuilt and extended it
- ❌ "The Fall 2025 P2P network is part of what we built" — completely separate codebase and team
- ❌ Any quantitative performance claim (latency, throughput numbers) — none measured and recorded

## 15. Final Mental Model

The MetaML Workbench is a **BPMN-driven process platform** that proves one end-to-end loop: capture a business process visually → generate runnable code → run it → mirror it with an automated twin → govern what the twin can do.

The Workbench runs three concurrent things: a React modeling frontend (bpmn-js), a Spring Boot + Camunda 7 backend (the Workbench engine), and an optional Node Manager stub (static agent catalog). When a user models a BPMN process and generates it, a complete Spring Boot + Camunda application is assembled from a template and launched as a separate child JVM with its own port. When a user deploys a Twin, the Workbench generates a transformed BPMN (User Tasks → Receive/Service Task pairs) and starts both Original and Twin as Camunda process instances inside the same engine.

The central technical mechanism: **`AutoBridgeTrigger`** listens on Camunda's own `ExecutionEvent` after each commit (`AFTER_COMMIT`), dispatches a bridge call on a dedicated thread, correlates the Twin's matching Receive Task, runs the automation synchronously, and writes the agent's outputs back onto the Original. The correctness of this mechanism required 8 evolutionary stages to establish empirically, with three Phase 7.5 findings corrected through independent adversarial re-review after the first implementation of each was found wrong. The governance system has two layers: a runtime-only platform quota (deny-list + per-twin budgets via `AtomicInteger`s) and a durable tenant policy engine (Tenant → Policy → Version → Rule → ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL) backed by JSON files and evaluated by `PolicyDecisionEngine`.

What this is not: it is not the broader MetaML P2P ecosystem, not a real agent marketplace, not production-hardened, and not a tool with real authentication. It is one demonstrable, tested, architecturally-reasoned slice of that broader vision — the "capture → twin → evolve → govern" loop — implemented with rigor unusual for a semester project, with every non-obvious decision traced back to empirical evidence rather than documentation assumption.

2. Key Technical Concepts:

**System Architecture:**
- MetaML: multi-semester NYU ITP platform for decentralized AI component discovery/sharing over P2P network
- MetaML Workbench: Team 3's implementation — BPMN modeling → code generation → digital twin → governance
- Three running processes: React SPA (port 3000), WbapiApplication/Camunda (port 8082), NodeManager stub (port 8083)
- Generated Target Platforms launched as separate child JVMs with dynamic ports

**BPMN Tooling:**
- bpmn-js 18 (browser-side BPMN editor)
- bpmn-js-properties-panel 5.62.0 (properties panel integration)
- camunda-bpmn-moddle 7.0.1 (Camunda namespace support in bpmn-js)
- camunda-bpmn-js-behaviors 1.18.0 (Camunda-specific modeler behaviors)
- bpmn-js-token-simulation 0.40.0 (token simulation UI)
- Camunda 7.22.0 process engine (server-side, `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter`)
- Camunda 7.22.0 webapp (Cockpit/Tasklist/Admin at /camunda, `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter-webapp`)
- `camunda-bpm-model` API (Camunda's own Java library for BPMN model manipulation)
- Camunda `metaml:` extension namespace for `metaml:dataItems`, `metaml:agentOutputs`

**Digital Twin Runtime:**
- `TwinModelGenerator`: transforms Original BPMN → Twin BPMN (User Task → Receive Task + Service Task)
- `AutoBridgeTrigger`: `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)` on Camunda's `ExecutionEvent`
- Spring's `EventPublisherPlugin` (Camunda Spring Boot Starter) republishes Camunda engine events into Spring bus
- Dedicated single-thread `ExecutorService` ("auto-bridge") for bridge dispatch
- `messageEventReceived(messageName, executionId)` for parallel multi-instance sibling targeting
- `HistoricDetail.variableUpdates()` for restart-safe visit deduplication
- `runtimeService.createIncident(...)` for incident-driven failure handling
- `enableDuplicateFiltering(true)` for deterministic Twin BPMN deployment reuse

**Synchronization Mechanisms (TWO DISTINCT):**
1. In-process (Workbench Original↔Twin bridge): `AFTER_COMMIT` event → dedicated executor thread → `bridgeActivityEvent()` → `messageEventReceived()` targeting specific execution ID. Event-driven, no polling.
2. Cross-process (Generated Target Platform Proxy↔Twin): `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000ms)` `SignalBroadcaster` polls Camunda event subscriptions → detects shared signal state → publishes to RabbitMQ queue → consumer executes → response queue → Proxy advances. 1-second polling.

**Governance (Two Layers):**
- Platform layer (`GovernanceServiceImpl`): deny-list + evolution budget (default 25) + execution budget (default 200). Runtime-only: `AtomicInteger` maps, reset on restart. `ConcurrentHashMap` keyed by twin ID.
- Tenant layer (`PolicyDecisionEngine`/`TenantPolicyService`): Tenant → Policy → PolicyVersion (DRAFT/ACTIVE/RETIRED) → PolicyRule (field, operator, value) → PolicyEffect (ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL). Durable via `TenantPolicyStore` JSON.
- Approvals: `ApprovalService`/`ApprovalStore` JSON persistence. REQUIRE_APPROVAL creates pending row; operator approve/reject executes pinned decision.

**Code Generation:**
- `DelegateClassGenerator`: Java class generation from BPMN delegate expressions, collision detection
- `ExternalTaskWorkerGenerator`: External task worker generation
- `TargetPlatformSourceGenerator`: XML DOM manipulation (javax.xml), generates Spring @Component beans
- `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator`: Generates SignalBroadcaster, PairRegistry, RabbitMQ queue pairs, controllers
- `TargetPlatformTwinMirrorGenerator`: Twin mirror component generation
- `SpringBootProjectGenerator`: Orchestrates all generation from template directory

**Node Manager (Three Concepts):**
1. `NodeManagerClient` (workbench library): HTTP GET to localhost:8083, 1s connect/2s read timeouts, RestTemplate
2. `nodemanager` stub (Spring Boot 3.5.16, port 8083): `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix="nodemanager")` YAML-backed, static catalog with 5 agent types
3. Real P2P Node Manager: in `p2p_fall25` codebase, NOT integrated, lives elsewhere

**Persistence:**
- Camunda H2 file DB: `jdbc:h2:file:./data/camunda` — durable Camunda engine state
- `WorkbenchStateStore`: JSON (models, twins) — durable
- `TenantPolicyStore`: JSON (tenants, policies, versions, rules) — durable
- `ApprovalStore`: JSON (approvals) — durable
- `WorkflowEventStore`: JSON (stage events) — durable
- Generated-project registry: reconstructed at startup from filesystem + WorkflowEventStore
- Platform governance counters: in-memory only (`ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>`) — runtime-only, deliberate

**Testing:**

**Frontend:**

**Camunda discovered limitations (from EVOLUTION_TIMELINE.md):**
- `camunda-bpm-model` 7.22.0 has no `AdHocSubProcess` class (confirmed via `javap`) — hard library limit
- Non-local vs. local `loopCounter` scope asymmetry between Original and Twin sides (proven by probe)
- `ProcessDefinition.getId()` occasionally omits composite shape in 7.22.0 under certain deployment patterns

## Section 6 — Digital Twin Runtime Technology Audit

| Technology / Mechanism | Evidence | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **`TwinModelGenerator`** (`@Component`) | `TwinModelGenerator.java` imports + class comment | Transforms Original BPMN → Twin BPMN: every UserTask becomes ReceiveTask + ServiceTask pair; handles ParallelGateway, ExclusiveGateway, BoundaryEvent, MultiInstance |
| **`TargetPlatformTwinMirrorGenerator`** (`@Component`) | `TargetPlatformTwinMirrorGenerator.java` | Mirror-generates Twin BPMN for generated Target Platforms by copying Proxy BPMN and suffixing process ID + external task topics (`camunda:topic` + "Twin") |
| **`AutoBridgeTrigger`** (`@Component`) | `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` | `@TransactionalEventListener(phase=AFTER_COMMIT)` listener — receives `ExecutionEvent` from Spring bus, dispatches to dedicated executor |
| **Dedicated Single-Thread `ExecutorService`** | `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` | `Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()` named "auto-bridge" — serializes bridge operations; `AtomicReference<ExecutorService>` for timeout-and-replace pattern; 6-second timeout per operation |
| **`Spring EventPublisherPlugin`** | Camunda Spring Boot Starter | Republishes Camunda engine `ExecutionEvent` into Spring `ApplicationEvent` bus — the bridge connecting Camunda's internal event system to Spring's |
| **`HistoricDetail.variableUpdates()`** | Camunda History API | Restart-safe visit deduplication — counts variable update sets per twin activity, not in-memory (lost on restart) |
| **`runtimeService.messageEventReceived(messageName, executionId)`** | Camunda Runtime API | Targets specific parallel sibling execution; found via `javap` inspection after `MessageCorrelationBuilder` approaches failed |
| **`resolveParallelSibling`** | Team-written | Walks ActivityInstance tree to find sibling execution with matching `loopCounter` — required for parallel multi-instance disambiguation |
| **`enableDuplicateFiltering(true)`** | Camunda Deployment API | Prevents redundant Twin re-deployment — requires `stabilize*` methods to ensure XML is deterministic |
| **`runtimeService.createIncident(...)`** | Camunda Runtime API | Incident-Driven failure policy — twin activity failure creates Camunda incident instead of automatic retry (no idempotency contract on `ProjectAutomationService.execute()`) |
| **Transaction rollback on failure** | Spring/Camunda transactional | Proven empirically: failed synchronous Camunda command rolls back the entire command including the Receive Task correlation, leaving twin wait state intact and safe to retry |
| **BPMN DI stripping** | `stripDiagramInterchange` | Removes non-deterministic BPMN diagram interchange elements from Twin XML to achieve byte-for-byte reproducibility |
| **`metaml:` namespace attributes** | Custom BPMN extension | `metaml:dataItems`, `metaml:agentOutputs` on process/task elements — carries data item / agent output schemas through the model |

---

## Section 7 — Synchronization / Messaging Technology Audit

**Two distinct sync mechanisms exist:**

### Mechanism 1: In-Process Original ↔ Twin Bridge (Workbench)

| Technology | Evidence | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **Spring `@TransactionalEventListener`** | `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` | `phase = AFTER_COMMIT` — fires after Original-side activity transaction commits |
| **`fallbackExecution = true`** | `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` | Fires even outside a transaction context |
| **`EventPublisherPlugin`** (Camunda Spring Boot Starter) | wbapi runtime | Bridges Camunda's internal `ExecutionEvent` into Spring's event bus |
| **Single-thread `ExecutorService`** | `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` | Serializes bridge dispatches; `AtomicReference` for 6-second timeout-and-replace |
| **`messageEventReceived(messageName, executionId)`** | Camunda Runtime API | Direct execution targeting for parallel sibling disambiguation |
| **Transport** | In-process method call | No network, no queue — pure JVM |
| **Pattern** | Event-driven, no polling | Original commits → Spring event → executor thread → bridge → Twin advances |

### Mechanism 2: Cross-Process Proxy ↔ Twin Sync (Generated Target Platforms)

| Technology | Evidence | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **RabbitMQ** | `RedCollarTP/pom.xml`, `application.properties`, `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` | AMQP message broker — required for Demo 5 |
| **`spring-boot-starter-amqp`** | `RedCollarTP/pom.xml` | Spring AMQP client — `RabbitTemplate`, `@RabbitListener` |
| **`@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000ms)`** | `TEAM_DEMO_GUIDE.md`, generated `SignalBroadcaster` | 1-second polling loop — checks Camunda event subscriptions for shared signal state |
| **`SignalBroadcaster`** (generated class) | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` | Polls Camunda → detects shared signal → publishes to RabbitMQ queue → consumer executes → response queue → Proxy advances |
| **`PairRegistry`** (generated class) | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` | `ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>` mapping businessKey → paired execution; pairs Proxy + Twin by same `businessKey` |
| **Per-signal RabbitMQ queue pairs** | code generation | Queue naming: scoped by `messagingNamespace` (projectId) + signal name |
| **AMQP retry** | `application.properties` | `spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.retry.enabled=true; max-attempts=30` |
| **`metaml.messaging.enabled`** | `application.properties` | Feature flag — `false` for `camundademo`, `true` for `RedCollarTP` |
| **Transport** | AMQP over TCP (localhost:5672) | RabbitMQ process — must be running separately |
| **Pattern** | Polling + queue | `@Scheduled` 1-second poll → AMQP message → AMQP response |

**Docker usage for RabbitMQ:** README states `docker start metaml-rabbitmq` — the RabbitMQ container itself is managed by Docker (pre-existing container named `metaml-rabbitmq`), but no Docker configuration is in the repository. RabbitMQ is an **external dependency**, not containerized as part of this project.

| Store | Technology | Location | Durability | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Camunda engine state** | H2 file-mode database | `backend/wbapi/data/camunda.mv.db` | Durable — survives restart | `application.properties`: `jdbc:h2:file:./data/camunda;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1` |
| **BPMN models / workflow state** | `WorkbenchStateStore` (whole-file JSON) | `backend/wbapi/data/` | Durable | `WorkflowEventStore` JSON |
| **Tenant policies** | `TenantPolicyStore` (whole-file JSON) | `backend/wbapi/data/` | Durable | Tenant → Policy → PolicyVersion → PolicyRule chain |
| **Approvals** | `ApprovalStore` (whole-file JSON) | `backend/wbapi/data/` | Durable | Pending/approved/rejected rows |
| **Workflow stage events** | `WorkflowEventStore` (whole-file JSON) | `backend/wbapi/data/` | Durable | Used to reconstruct generated-project registry on startup |
| **Generated project registry** | Reconstructed at startup | in-memory, rebuilt from `WorkflowEventStore` + filesystem scan | In-memory (rebuilt from durable sources) | README: "no persistence layer to recover launched JVMs" |
| **Platform governance counters** | `ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>` | in-memory only | **Volatile — resets on restart** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java`; documented in README known limitations #8 |
| **H2 JDBC driver** | `org.h2.Driver` | `application.properties` | — | Explicit driver class declaration |
| **camundademo template DB** | H2 in-memory | `jdbc:h2:mem:process-engine;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1` | In-memory — lost on shutdown | `templates/camundademo/application.properties` |
| **RedCollarTP DB** | H2 in-memory | `jdbc:h2:mem:camunda;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1` | In-memory — generated project state lost on shutdown | `RedCollarTP/application.properties` |
| **Jackson** | (from Spring Boot) | JSON serialization | — | Used for all JSON state store read/write |

**Explicit non-technology:** No Redis, no PostgreSQL, no MongoDB, no Elasticsearch, no Flyway/Liquibase migrations. All persistence is either Camunda's own H2 schema management or team-written whole-file JSON.

## Section 9 — Code Generation Technology Audit

| Generator Class | Technology Used | What It Generates | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`DelegateClassGenerator`** | Camunda `BpmnModelInstance` model API (`Bpmn.readModelFromStream(...)`) | Java delegate class source (`.java`) per unique `delegateExpression` found on `ServiceTask` + `UserTask.taskListener`. Deduped by class name (not bean name). Package name = caller-supplied (matches Spring `@ComponentScan` root) | `DelegateClassGenerator.java` imports: `org.camunda.bpm.model.*`, `ByteArrayInputStream`, `StandardCharsets` |
| **`ExternalTaskWorkerGenerator`** | Template string manipulation | External task worker Java class source | `SpringBootProjectGenerator.java` orchestration |
| **`TargetPlatformSourceGenerator`** | Java `javax.xml` DOM (`DocumentBuilderFactory`, `TransformerFactory`, `DOMSource`, `StreamResult`) | Spring `@Component` delegate beans from BPMN delegate expressions; inserts signal catch events for lockstep sync (`sync_<activityId>`, prefix `SYNC_SIGNAL_PREFIX = "sync_"`) | `TargetPlatformSourceGenerator.java` imports: `javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory`, `javax.xml.XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING` |
| **`TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator`** | Java `javax.xml` DOM + template strings | `PairRegistry` (`ConcurrentHashMap<String,String>`), `SignalBroadcaster` (`@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)`), RabbitMQ configuration, proxy/twin controllers, per-signal queue pairs | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` |
| **`TargetPlatformTwinMirrorGenerator`** | Java `javax.xml` DOM | Twin BPMN by copying Proxy BPMN and applying two changes: `_twin` suffix on process ID/name, `Twin` suffix on all `camunda:topic` attributes | `TargetPlatformTwinMirrorGenerator.java` |
| **`SpringBootProjectGenerator`** | Filesystem template copy (`RedCollarTP/` or `camundademo/`) + generator orchestration | Complete Maven project directory — copies template, applies all generators above, writes all `.java` files, writes `pom.xml`, writes `application.properties` | `SpringBootProjectGenerator.java` |
| **`SpringBootProjectLauncher`** | `ProcessBuilder` (or equivalent shell-out to `mvn`) | Launches `mvn clean install` then `mvn spring-boot:run` as separate child JVM | `SpringBootProjectLauncherMavenInstallTest` (the 1 failing test — requires system `mvn`) |
| **Template directory** | Filesystem | `../RedCollarTP` (default per `application.properties`) — the actual source tree cloned as project skeleton | `application.properties`: `workbench.generation.template-directory=../RedCollarTP` |
| **Output directory** | Filesystem | `../../../generated-target-platforms/` — peer directory to repository root | `application.properties`: `workbench.generation.output-directory` |
| **XML security** | `XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING` | XXE protection on all XML DOM parsing in codegen | All generator files that use `DocumentBuilderFactory` |

**Key code generation facts:**
- Delegate class name comes from `delegateExpression` value (e.g. `${calculateInterestService}` → `CalculateInterestService`), NOT from task display name — Camunda resolves the expression, not the label
- Collision detection: two different `delegateExpression` values that sanitize to the same Java class name are caught; the offending element ID is returned for frontend error display (Demo 2)
- The `camundademo` template is not the default at runtime — `application.properties` points to `../RedCollarTP`

## Section 10 — Governance Technology Audit

### Layer 1: Platform Governance

| Technology | Evidence | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **`GovernanceServiceImpl`** (`@Component`) | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Runtime-only platform-level governance |
| **`volatile Set<String> deniedAgentTypes`** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Deny-list — agents blocked platform-wide |
| **`volatile int maxEvolutionsPerTwin`** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Default 25 (from `application.properties` comments) |
| **`volatile int maxTwinExecutionsPerTwin`** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Default 200 |
| **`ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>`** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Per-twin evolution and execution counters |
| **Increment-then-rollback pattern** | `GovernanceServiceImpl.java` | Avoids check-then-increment race: increments first, rolls back if limit exceeded — race-safe |
| **Deliberate in-memory-only** | README known limitation #8 | Platform quota intentionally resets on restart — documented design decision |

### Layer 2: Tenant Policy Governance

| Technology | Evidence | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **`PolicyDecisionEngine`** | `PolicyDecisionEngine.java` | Evaluates tenant + platform policies — platform wins on ties; default ALLOW if no matching rule |
| **`TenantPolicyService`** | domain service | Tenant → Policy → PolicyVersion (DRAFT/ACTIVE/RETIRED) → PolicyRule (field/operator/value) → PolicyEffect (ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL) |
| **`TenantPolicyStore`** | JSON file persistence | Durable (survives restart) — whole-file JSON |
| **Policy operators** | `PolicyDecisionEngine.java` | `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` |
| **`PolicyEffect.REQUIRE_APPROVAL`** | `ApprovalService.java` | Creates pending approval row; operator approve/reject executes pinned decision |
| **`ApprovalStore`** | JSON file persistence | Durable — whole-file JSON |
| **Tenant ID** | caller-supplied string | Unauthenticated — no verification, by deliberate design; UI discloses this |

## Section 16 — Architecture Mechanisms vs. Technologies

**Two separate lists — mechanism describes what; technology describes how.**

### Architecture Mechanisms (what the system does)

1. BPMN capture → Save → Generate → Launch lifecycle
2. Original ↔ Twin automatic bridge (AFTER_COMMIT synchronization)
3. Parallel multi-instance sibling disambiguation
4. Restart-safe visit deduplication (HistoricDetail-based)
5. Incident-driven twin failure policy
6. Platform governance (deny-list + evolution/execution budgets)
7. Tenant policy governance (ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL with PolicyVersions)
8. Cross-process Proxy↔Twin lockstep synchronization via signal events
9. Delegate class name collision detection with element-level error attribution
10. Duplicate-filtered Twin BPMN deployment (deterministic XML)
11. Node Manager agent catalog lookup
12. Whole-file JSON persistence for mutable system state
13. Generated-project registry reconstruction at startup

### Technologies Implementing Those Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Technology |
|---|---|
| BPMN capture | bpmn-js 18 + bpmn-js-properties-panel 5.62.0 + camunda-bpmn-moddle 7.0.1 |
| Original→Twin bridge | Spring `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` + Camunda `EventPublisherPlugin` + `Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()` + `messageEventReceived(name, execId)` |
| Parallel sibling disambiguation | `ActivityInstance` tree walk + `runtimeService.messageEventReceived(messageName, executionId)` |
| Restart-safe visit deduplication | `historyService.createHistoricDetailQuery().variableUpdates()` |
| Twin failure policy | `runtimeService.createIncident(...)` + Camunda incident management |
| Platform governance | `ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>` + `volatile` fields + increment-then-rollback |
| Tenant policy governance | `TenantPolicyStore` JSON + `PolicyDecisionEngine` + `ApprovalStore` JSON |
| Cross-process sync | RabbitMQ AMQP + `spring-boot-starter-amqp` + `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)` + generated `SignalBroadcaster` + `PairRegistry` (`ConcurrentHashMap`) |
| Collision detection | `camunda-bpm-model` `Bpmn.readModelFromStream()` + `LinkedHashMap` dedup-by-className |
| Duplicate-filtered Twin deploy | `enableDuplicateFiltering(true)` + `stabilizeMessageIds` / `stabilizeMultiInstanceIds` / `stripDiagramInterchange` |
| Node Manager lookup | `RestTemplate` (1s/2s timeout) + `@ConfigurationProperties` YAML-backed stub |
| JSON persistence | Jackson `ObjectMapper` + whole-file read/write pattern |
| Registry reconstruction | `WorkflowEventStore` JSON replay + filesystem scan |

**The `application.properties` and the actual generated projects on disk disagree.**

- `wbapi/application.properties` line 83: `workbench.generation.template-directory=../RedCollarTP`

**Interpretation:** All four projects in `data/generated-projects/` — including the ones used for Demo 5 (verified 2026-08-23) — were generated from the `camundademo` template, not from `RedCollarTP`. The `application.properties` setting was changed to point to `../RedCollarTP` at some point after these projects were generated.

**Authoritative version for "what the demos actually ran":** Spring Boot **4.1.0**, Camunda **7.24.0**, Java **24** (the camundademo template).

**Authoritative version for "what a new generation would produce today":** RedCollarTP template — Spring Boot **3.1.12**, Camunda **7.20.0**, Java **17** — if `application.properties` is taken at face value.

**This is a genuine split: the demo evidence and the current configuration point to different versions.**

### Conflict 2: Maven version — three different wrappers

- `backend/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: **3.9.11** (used by `./mvnw` from `backend/`)
- `backend/wbapi/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: **3.9.16**
- `backend/workbench/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: **3.9.16**
- `backend/RedCollarTP/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: **3.9.6**
- `data/generated-projects/*/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties`: **3.9.16**

**Authoritative version:** The README instructs running from `backend/` using `./mvnw`, which uses the `backend/.mvn/wrapper/` file → **3.9.11**. The per-module wrappers (3.9.16) appear to be residual from Spring Initializr generation and would only activate if running mvnw from within those subdirectories directly. Neither is an error; they are independent wrapper files. For the poster: Maven is a build tool and should not appear on the poster regardless.

### Conflict 3: `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter` not directly in `wbapi`

`wbapi/pom.xml` only declares `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter-webapp` (version 7.22.0). The core `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter` (version 7.22.0) is declared in `workbench/pom.xml`. `wbapi` gets the core starter **transitively** via its dependency on the `workbench` library. Both resolve to Camunda 7.22.0, so there is no functional conflict — but the dependency structure is: `wbapi → workbench (pom dep) → camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter 7.22.0`.

### Conflict 4: camundademo template dependency list is Spring Initializr bloat

The `templates/camundademo/pom.xml` (and therefore all actual generated projects in `data/`) includes an enormous list of Spring Boot starters (`spring-boot-starter-restclient`, `spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-*`, `spring-boot-starter-mail`, `spring-boot-starter-websocket`, `spring-rabbit-stream`, `spring-boot-starter-actuator`, `spring-data-rest-hal-explorer`, etc.) and multiple test starters (`spring-boot-starter-actuator-test`, `spring-boot-starter-amqp-test`, etc.) that are almost certainly Spring Initializr auto-generated boilerplate. The note in `application.properties` about RedCollarTP being more intentional suggests the team knows the generated template is over-specified. For the poster: this does not change the versions, but it means the generated TP pom.xml includes far more dependencies than the project actually uses.

### Conflict 5: Frontend declared ranges vs. installed versions

`package.json` declares `^19.2.7` for React (meaning ≥19.2.7, <20.0.0). Without a `package-lock.json`, the exact installed version is not committed to the repository. The actual React version in `node_modules/` on this machine cannot be determined from checked-in files alone. Same applies to every other frontend package. **For the poster, only state the declared minimum version floor, not an exact version.**

## 6. IMPORTANT CORRECTIONS TO PREVIOUS AUDIT

The following statements from the Phase 2 exhaustive audit (previous response) were wrong, insufficiently verified, or now require qualification:

**Correction 1 — Generated TP versions were stated with complete confidence as RedCollarTP's versions. This was wrong.**

Previous audit stated:
> "RedCollarTP: Spring Boot 3.1.12 / Camunda 7.20.0 / Java 17 (DIFFERENT versions from wbapi)"
> "Generated-project runtime versions (Java 17, Spring Boot 3.1.12, Camunda 7.20.0)"

**Actual finding:** Every generated project in `data/generated-projects/` (4 projects, all examined) uses **Spring Boot 4.1.0 / Camunda 7.24.0 / Java 24** — the camundademo template, not RedCollarTP. The previous audit read `application.properties` and `RedCollarTP/pom.xml` and inferred they reflected what was actually generated. It did not read the actual generated project pom.xml files. Reading those files reveals they contradict the application.properties configuration.

**Correction 2 — `camundademo` was characterized as "experimental/future" and "not the current default."**

Previous audit stated:
> "camundademo is not the current default (RedCollarTP is)"
> "camundademo — alternate generation template (future/experimental)"

**Actual finding:** The camundademo template IS what all actual generated projects were built from. RedCollarTP may be the current *configured* template (per `application.properties`), but it is not what produced the demo evidence on disk. The characterization of camundademo as future/experimental was inaccurate given the evidence.

**Correction 3 — `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter` was listed as a direct `wbapi` dependency.**

Previous audit listed it under "Backend: `wbapi` module" as a direct dependency. **Actual finding:** `wbapi/pom.xml` only directly declares `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter-webapp` (7.22.0). The core `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter` is in `workbench/pom.xml`. `wbapi` gets it transitively via `workbench`.

**Correction 4 — `wbapi` has more declared dependencies than the previous audit listed.**

Missed from `wbapi/pom.xml`: `spring-boot-starter-data-rest`, `spring-boot-starter-hateoas`, `spring-boot-starter-mail`, `spring-boot-starter-validation`, `spring-data-rest-hal-explorer`, `spring-boot-devtools`, `jakarta.ws.rs-api 4.0.0`, `spring-security-test`. These were in the pom.xml but not captured in the previous audit.

**Correction 5 — `redux` was said to be in `package.json`. Confirmed — but it is `react-redux` (^9.2.0) and `redux-thunk` (^3.1.0), not `redux` standalone.** The previous audit listed `redux` as a dependency; the actual package.json does not have a bare `redux` entry. It has `react-redux: ^9.2.0` and `redux-thunk: ^3.1.0`.

**Correction 6 — Additional frontend dependencies missed in previous audit.**

`package.json` also contains: `@fortawesome/*`, `chart.js`, `chartist`, `datatables.net-*`, `jquery`, `react-chartjs-2`, `react-data-table-component`, `react-datepicker`, `react-helmet`, `react-icons`, `react-slick`, `recharts`, `redux-thunk`, `styled-components`, `simplebar-react`, `content-security-policy`. These are unremarkable utility packages but they were not listed.

**Correction 7 — Maven version was stated as 3.9.11 for the workbench build.** This is correct for the aggregator wrapper (`backend/.mvn/wrapper/`) but the individual module wrappers (`wbapi/.mvn/wrapper/`, `workbench/.mvn/wrapper/`) both declare **3.9.16**. The previous audit stated "3.9.11" without noting the per-module wrapper discrepancy.

**Correction 8 — bpmn-js-token-simulation was characterized as uncertain ("if actually used").** It is declared in `package.json`. Usage was not confirmed in source files read, but its presence in dependencies and not being behind a feature flag is sufficient basis for inclusion. Not a factual error, but a precision note.

---

## Demo Guide

Full click-by-click transcripts are in [`TEAM_DEMO_GUIDE.md`](TEAM_DEMO_GUIDE.md). Fixtures are in [`demo/`](demo/). Summary of what each demo proves:

| Demo | Fixture | What it shows | RabbitMQ needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Demo 1** | `demo/wire-transfer-review.bpmn` | Model → Save → Generate → Launch → Stop lifecycle; survives reload and backend restart | No |
| **Demo 2** | `demo/settlement-collision.bpmn` | Element-aware error recovery: two delegates collide → RED banner → "Go to error" highlights the offending element → rename → GREEN | No |
| **Demo 3** | `demo/wire-transfer-review-BROKEN.bpmn` | Global failure with no element blamed; no "Go to error" — contrast case for Demo 2 | No |
| **Demo 4** | `demo/wire-transfer-review-twin.bpmn` | Tenant → Policy → Draft → Rule → Activate → Deploy Twin → Connect → Evolve → approval queue | No |
| **Demo 5** | `demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn` + `demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn` | Proxy↔Twin lockstep synchronization over RabbitMQ; verified 2026-08-23 (9/9 workers, both instances completed) | **Yes** — `docker start metaml-rabbitmq` first |

---

**Two things to know before any demo:**
- **Opening a BPMN file does not save it.** Import only means bpmn-js read the XML. Camunda validation happens at **Save**.
- **Save never overwrites.** Every Save creates a new model ID by design.

**For Demo 5 only**, start RabbitMQ first, then launch Proxy and Twin back-to-back with the **same `businessKey`**. A Proxy-only run completes normally and never touches RabbitMQ — that's expected but proves nothing about synchronization.

---

**Windows-specific traps (confirmed empirically):**
- Always use `.\` prefix — bare `mvnw.cmd` fails with "not recognized" even in the right directory
- Never add `-am` to the `spring-boot:run` invocation — Maven applies the goal to `workbench` too, which has no main class, and fails before `wbapi` starts
- **Do not restart the backend mid-demo** — launched child JVMs keep their port but become invisible to the Workbench

COLUMN 1

[Section: The Problem]
Enterprises cannot introduce AI capabilities into live business processes without halting, rewriting, or replacing them. Retrofitting AI into a running workflow risks breaking established logic, disrupting live operations, and bypassing compliance controls. No standard tooling exists to evolve a deployed process incrementally, with governance, while keeping the original untouched.

[Section: Our Solution]
The MetaML Workbench lets an organization capture any business process visually, deploy it to a live process engine, and automatically generate a synchronized Digital Twin that runs alongside it. The Twin's activities are driven by pluggable AI agents sourced from a decentralized network — introduced incrementally, constrained by a two-layer governance system, and verified before any agent touches a live process.

The result: AI augmentation of a running business process without modifying, pausing, or redeploying the original.

[Section: How It Works — User Flow]
1. Draw or import a BPMN process in the visual Workbench editor
2. Save → the process is validated and deployed to a Camunda 7 engine
3. Generate → a complete Spring Boot application is produced from the diagram
4. Launch → the generated app runs as a live child JVM on a dynamic port
5. Deploy Twin → a Digital Twin process is automatically created and co-deployed
6. Evolve → assign AI agents to Twin activities through the Node Manager
7. Govern → every agent request passes through deny-list and policy enforcement before execution

---

COLUMN 2

[Section: System Architecture]

BPMN Modeling Layer
Users work in a React 19 frontend powered by bpmn-js 18. The editor is extended with a custom MetaML namespace (metaml:dataItems, metaml:agentOutputs) that annotates tasks and processes with structured data definitions — information Camunda's own schema does not carry. Saved models are validated by the Camunda 7 engine before deployment.

Code Generation Layer
The Workbench derives a complete Maven project from the BPMN diagram. Java delegate classes are generated from delegateExpression values (not display names — the expression is what Camunda resolves at runtime). RabbitMQ queue pairs, a SignalBroadcaster polling coordinator, and a PairRegistry for process pairing are all generated automatically from the BPMN signal structure.

Digital Twin Runtime
TwinModelGenerator transforms every User Task in the original process into a ReceiveTask + ServiceTask pair in the Twin — the ReceiveTask holds the token as a genuine wait state (no job executor interference), and the ServiceTask executes the assigned agent. Original-to-Twin synchronization fires via Spring's @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) on a dedicated single-thread executor — event-driven, zero polling, zero added latency.

Cross-Process Synchronization
When the generated Target Platform runs as a separate JVM, a @Scheduled(1-second) SignalBroadcaster polls Camunda event subscriptions, detects shared signal state, and relays it over RabbitMQ AMQP. The Twin and Proxy processes advance in lockstep through each shared activity boundary.

Governance Layer
Enforcement runs at two layers before any agent executes:
• Platform layer: a runtime deny-list of agent types + per-twin evolution budget (default 25) and execution budget (default 200), backed by thread-safe atomic counters with increment-then-rollback race safety
• Tenant policy layer: full policy lifecycle (DRAFT → ACTIVE → RETIRED), rule evaluation with six comparison operators, three enforcement effects (ALLOW / DENY / REQUIRE_APPROVAL), and a durable approval queue that persists across restarts

---

✓ Cross-Process Lockstep Synchronization
Proxy and Twin processes advance activity-by-activity over RabbitMQ. Verified 2026-08-23: 7 activities, 9/9 external task workers executed, both process instances completed to end event.

✓ Two-Layer Governance API
Platform deny-list + per-twin budgets enforced at the service layer. Tenant policy engine with versioned rules and an approval queue — all durable, all tested.

✓ Node Manager Integration

✓ 299 Automated Tests

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 4:38:53 AM</sup>

```
Assume you are a professional academic poster designer specializing in university research presentations.

Create a 4K (3840×2160px) NYU-branded 3-column academic poster as a single rendered image. Do not use LaTeX, Python, or any code — output the final image directly.

TITLE: MetaML — Decentralized Platform for Reusable, Evolvable Agents
SUBTITLE: A Twin-Process Platform for AI-Augmented Business Automation
AUTHORS: Emily Chen · Henry Weisman · Nirman Taterh
INSTITUTION: NYU ITP · Team 3 · Summer 2026

NYU BRAND COLORS:
- Header/footer background: #57068C (NYU Violet)
- Section headers: #330662 (NYU Dark Violet)
- Accent: #8900E1
- Body background: #F9F6FC
- Text: #1a1a1a on light, white on dark
- Include the NYU logo wordmark top-right in the header

---

COLUMN 1 — Company Description + Project Business Objectives

Company Description:
MetaML is a multi-semester NYU ITP research platform building a decentralized network for discovering, sharing, and reusing AI components — bots, models, and workflows — across peer-to-peer nodes. This team (Team 3, Summer 2026) owns the Workbench layer: capturing business processes visually, deploying them with synchronized Digital Twins, and governing AI agent injection at runtime. This is one working, demonstrable slice of the larger MetaML vision.

Project Business Objectives:
1. Enable organizations to augment running BPMN business processes with reusable AI agents — without rewriting or replacing the original system
2. Deploy each modeled process alongside an automatically generated Digital Twin that can introduce agents at specific activity boundaries
3. Enforce governance constraints (deny-list, per-twin budgets, tenant policies) before any agent is injected into a live process
4. Connect twin process activities to the MetaML P2P node manager to retrieve agents on demand
5. Deliver a fully demonstrable end-to-end loop: Model → Generate → Deploy → Twin → Evolve → Govern

---

COLUMN 2 — Business Architecture + Solution Details/Approach
(Focus on processes, organizational roles, and system interactions)

Business Architecture (use a clean layered diagram or flowchart):
- User / Business Analyst → BPMN Workbench (React frontend) → models the process visually
- Workbench → Spring Boot backend → deploys Original Process + auto-generates Digital Twin on Camunda
- Twin activities → Governance API → checks deny-list + per-twin budget + tenant policy → if ALLOW, contacts Node Manager Client
- Node Manager Client → MetaML Node Manager (stub, port 8083) → retrieves reusable agent/bot
- Agent executes inside Twin activity; Original Process runs unmodified in parallel
- RabbitMQ bridges cross-process signal choreography between Proxy JVM and Twin JVM

Solution Details / Approach:
- BPMN Workbench: React + bpmn-js 18 with custom metaml: namespace for task/process data Camunda doesn't natively carry
- Twin Generation: TwinModelGenerator transforms every UserTask into a ReceiveTask + ServiceTask pair; bridge fires on AFTER_COMMIT, zero polling
- Governance: two-layer — platform deny-list + per-twin evolution quota (in-memory) + tenant policies (JSON-persisted, ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL)
- Node Manager: HTTP client with 1s/2s timeout connecting to a 5-agent stub catalog (YAML-backed)
- Cross-process sync: SignalBroadcaster @Scheduled(1s), per-signal RabbitMQ queue pairs, Proxy↔Twin lockstep verified

---

COLUMN 3 — Business Value Achieved + Lessons Learned / Next Steps

Business Value Achieved:
1. End-to-end BPMN workbench delivered — visual process modeling with task/process data, full Model → Save → Generate → Launch → Stop lifecycle working and demo-verified
2. Working Digital Twin deployment — Original and Twin run in parallel on the same Camunda engine; activity-level synchronization proven with 299 tests (216 domain, 77 API, 6 node manager)
3. Two-layer governance enforced — deny-list + per-twin budgets + tenant ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL policies, with an approval queue UI
4. Connected node manager client — twin activities retrieve agents from the MetaML stub catalog on demand; 5 agent types, YAML-backed
5. Cross-process RabbitMQ sync demonstrated — Proxy↔Twin lockstep verified in live demo (9/9 workers executed, 2026-08-23)

Lessons Learned / Next Steps:
Lessons Learned:
- Camunda's Job Executor interferes with async Service Tasks — Receive Task wait-state design was critical to correctness
- Non-deterministic BPMN builder IDs silently break duplicate-filtering — explicit ID stabilization required
- "Done" without adversarial review is not done — 3 of 4 W4 fix attempts were wrong before the final solution

Next Steps:
- Real P2P Node Manager integration (replace stub)
- MCP-compliant MetaML API endpoint (Task 2, not yet started)
- Governance quota persistence across restarts
- KMP → A2A / ACP / ANP protocol compatibility (Tasks 4–5)
- VS Code plugin with MetaML API integration (Task 6)

---

LAYOUT RULES:
- Three equal columns separated by subtle dividers
- Each column has a bold NYU Violet (#57068C) section header matching the professor's exact labels above
- Use numbered or bulleted lists, not dense paragraphs
- Business Architecture column should include a simple process/org flow diagram
- Footer: "NYU ITP · Team 3 · Summer 2026 · metaml_su_2026" centered, white on violet
- Poster dimensions: 120cm × 72cm landscape equivalent at 4K resolution
- No placeholder text — all content above must appear in the final image
```

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 4:52:16 AM</sup>

The BMC is a well-established standard (Osterwalder & Pigneur, 2010) — I know it well. Here's the canonical structure:

---

## Business Model Canvas — 9 Blocks

The BMC is a single-page visual with a **fixed layout** — not a free-form poster. The standard arrangement:

```
┌─────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────┐
│ Key         │ Key          │ Value        │ Customer     │ Customer    │
│ Partners    │ Activities   │ Proposition  │ Relationships│ Segments    │
│             ├──────────────┤              ├──────────────┤             │
│             │ Key          │              │ Channels     │             │
│             │ Resources    │              │              │             │
├─────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┤
│            Cost Structure                │    Revenue Streams           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
```

### The 9 blocks explained:
1. **Key Partners** — who you work with (suppliers, alliances, other teams/semesters)
2. **Key Activities** — what you do to deliver value (BPMN modeling, twin generation, governance enforcement)
3. **Key Resources** — what you need (React frontend, Spring Boot, Camunda, RabbitMQ, dev team)
4. **Value Proposition** — what problem you solve and why you're different (center block — most important)
5. **Customer Relationships** — how you interact with users (self-service workbench, demo-guided, open source)
6. **Channels** — how you reach customers (GitHub, ITP showcase, faculty review)
7. **Customer Segments** — who you serve (enterprise teams, researchers, NYU ITP faculty/next teams)
8. **Cost Structure** — major costs (dev time, cloud infra, Camunda licensing considerations)
9. **Revenue Streams** — how value is captured (academic/research context: grants, platform licensing, future SaaS)

---

**Key rules for a proper BMC:**
- Fixed grid layout — blocks must be in the canonical positions above
- Value Proposition is the **center**, flanked by left side (supply) and right side (demand)
- Bottom row spans full width: Cost Structure (left) + Revenue Streams (right)
- Should be **one page**, landscape, visually dense but scannable
- NYU ITP context: Revenue/Cost can be framed as academic value / resource investment

Want me to now read the current `poster.tex` for the BMC and see how close Henry's version is, then write a ChatGPT prompt to fix or rebuild it?

- **Legal landscape:** 14" × 8.5" → 4200×2550px at 300 DPI
- **Tabloid:** 17" × 11" → 5100×3300px at 300 DPI (not a standard trifold size but doable)

MetaML Workbench is a BPMN-based environment for designing process workflows and generating executable runtime applications.

The central architectural idea is separation of:
- process definition
- execution intelligence

The intended runtime loop is:

MODEL → GENERATE → RUN → TWIN → GOVERN

The system should allow a BPMN process to be modeled, generated into a runnable process application, executed, synchronized with a Digital Twin, and governed when AI/agent actions occur.

102	
103	**The setup:** two service tasks carry different delegate expressions that sanitise to the *same*
104	Java class name, because `toClassName` maps every illegal identifier character to `_`:
105	
106	```
107	Task_SettleA   camunda:delegateExpression="${settle_payment}"   ->  Settle_payment
108	Task_SettleB   camunda:delegateExpression="${settle-payment}"   ->  Settle_payment
109	```
110	
111	Only one class file can be written. `Task_SettleA` is encountered first and names the class, so
112	**`Task_SettleB` is the element that loses** — its bean would silently never exist at runtime.
113	Camunda accepts both expressions at deploy time, so nothing upstream catches this. Generation is
114	the first and only place it can be caught.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 3:06:34 PM</sup>

The cleanest ways to show it live:

**1. Camunda Cockpit (best visual)**

Go to **http://localhost:8082/camunda** — login `demo`/`demo`

You'll see both the Original and Twin as live process instances. As the Original advances (you complete a user task via REST), the Twin's token moves in step. Joanna can see two separate process diagrams both progressing.

**2. REST calls in terminal — show the Original advancing**
```powershell
# complete a user task on the Original (replace {id} with actual task id)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8082/api/v1/wb/transmute/{processInstanceId}/review/complete
```
Then refresh Cockpit — both tokens move.

**3. Backend terminal logs (Tab 1)**

The `AutoBridgeTrigger` fires after each Original commit — you'll see log lines showing the bridge firing and the Twin advancing. Point to those logs while clicking through the Original's tasks.

**4. Twin Workflow page in the UI**

In the app: **Evolve → Twin Workflow** — shows the twin's status, connected activity, and evolution history in real time.

---

For the demo, the cleanest flow is:
1. Open Cockpit side by side with the app
2. Complete a task in the app
3. Show both tokens move in Cockpit

That's the most visually convincing proof of lockstep synchronization.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 3:06:48 PM</sup>

```powershell
# 1. Start a twin process - get the processInstanceId from the UI, then watch logs in Tab 1
# The AutoBridgeTrigger logs fire here every time Original advances

# 2. List running process instances
curl http://localhost:8082/api/v1/wb/twins

# 3. Complete a user task on the Original (advances it)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8082/api/v1/wb/transmute/{modelId}/tasks/{taskId}/complete

# 4. Poll twin state to show it moved in sync
curl http://localhost:8082/api/v1/wb/twins/{twinId}
```

The real proof is in **Tab 1 logs** — every time you complete a step on the Original, you'll see `AutoBridgeTrigger` fire immediately after, showing the Twin advancing. That's the lockstep in terminal form.

To get the actual IDs, run:
```powershell
curl http://localhost:8082/api/v1/wb/models
```
Then grab a `modelId` that has a twin launched.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 3:10:12 PM</sup>

The `SignalBroadcaster` lives in the **generated Target Platform** (cross-process, RabbitMQ side — not the Workbench itself). Here's what it does:

**Its job:** deliver BPMN signals to the specific Camunda executions waiting on them, so the Proxy and Twin can both advance past each shared signal point in lockstep.

**Why it exists:** In the generated Target Platform, the Proxy and Twin are two separate process instances. Neither throws its own signals — something external has to fire those signals to the right executions at the right time. That's the SignalBroadcaster.

**How it works:**
1. It polls every 1 second checking which signal catch events have executions currently waiting on them
2. For a **paired** Proxy+Twin (same `businessKey` via `PairRegistry`): it does a two-step handoff — sends a task message to Twin via RabbitMQ, waits for Twin's response, then releases the Proxy. Neither side advances until both are ready → true lockstep
3. For an **unpaired** instance (Proxy running alone, no Twin): delivers the signal directly so the Proxy can still complete normally
4. The `partnerNotComing` fallback: after 5 polling ticks with no partner arriving, it stops waiting and delivers directly

**To show Joanna in terminal:**
```powershell
# Start Proxy and Twin with the same businessKey
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/proxy/start?businessKey=demo1
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/twin/start?businessKey=demo1
```
Then watch Tab 1 logs — you'll see `SignalBroadcaster` logging each signal delivery and the RabbitMQ handoff between them.

## Part 1 — Email to Joanna

---

Hi Joanna,

Wanted to point you to where the RabbitMQ and Proxy/Twin communication pieces live in the repo, since I imagine you'll want to look at the implementation directly.

**Quick repo layout**

The backend splits into three modules under `backend/`:
- `workbench/` — all domain logic: BPMN modeling, code generation, twin runtime, governance. No web layer.
- `wbapi/` — the Spring Boot host, REST controllers, and embedded Camunda 7.22 engine.
- `nodemanager/` — a stub agent catalog (properties-file-backed, no real P2P).

The `backend/RedCollarTP/` directory is the generated Target Platform template — this is what gets copied and filled in when you click Generate for the Proxy/Twin scenario.

**RabbitMQ — what it is and what it isn't**

RabbitMQ is not part of the Workbench's internal synchronization. The Workbench's own Original↔Twin sync uses an `AFTER_COMMIT` Spring transaction event listener (`AutoBridgeTrigger.java` in `workbench/`) that fires after each Original activity commits and drives the Twin forward. No broker involved.

RabbitMQ lives entirely in the **generated Target Platform** — the separate Spring Boot application that gets synthesized from the Proxy and Twin BPMNs. All of it is code-generated, not hand-written, by `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` (`backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/`).

That generator writes five classes into each generated project under `src/main/java/com/tp/TargetPlatform/messaging/`:
- `RabbitMqConfig` — declares the exchange, and one task queue + one response queue per shared BPMN signal. Enabled only when `metaml.messaging.enabled=true`.
- `TaskQueuePublisher` — publishes to the task queue (Proxy side signals it's ready).
- `ResponseQueuePublisher` — publishes to the response queue (Twin side signals it completed).
- `TaskQueueListener` — `@RabbitListener` that consumes task messages and calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` to release the Twin's execution.
- `ResponseQueueListener` — `@RabbitListener` that consumes response messages and calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` to release the Proxy's execution.

Queue naming: each shared signal gets its own pair of queues namespaced to the generated project ID, so two independently generated platforms can never share a queue even if they have identically-named signals.

**Proxy↔Twin communication — the actual flow**

Pairing happens through `PairRegistry` (generated into `coordination/`). Both sides call their `/start?businessKey=X` endpoint with the same key. The first to register becomes the "initiator" (Proxy), the second becomes the "responder" (Twin).

The synchronization driver is `SignalBroadcaster` (generated into `signal/`), which runs on a `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)` — once per second. On each tick it queries Camunda for all executions currently waiting on each BPMN signal name, then decides what to do based on who's waiting:

Step by step for a paired Proxy+Twin both waiting on the same signal:

1. SignalBroadcaster sees both a Proxy execution and a Twin execution subscribed to the same signal.
2. **REQUEST**: it calls `deliverTo()` on the Twin (responder) first. If RabbitMQ is enabled, `TaskQueuePublisher.publish()` sends `"signalName|executionId|processInstanceId|businessKey"` to the task queue. `TaskQueueListener` consumes it and calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, twinExecutionId)` — Twin's signal catch event releases and its gated delegate runs synchronously in the same Camunda transaction.
3. SignalBroadcaster sets an `awaitingResponse` flag and does NOT release the Proxy yet. On the next tick it calls `responderHasAdvancedPast()`, which re-queries Camunda to check that Twin is no longer subscribed to that signal name — proof the gated task actually completed, not merely that the signal arrived.
4. **RESPONSE**: once confirmed, `deliverTo()` on the Proxy. If RabbitMQ is enabled, `ResponseQueuePublisher.publish()` sends to the response queue. `ResponseQueueListener` consumes it and calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, proxyExecutionId)` — Proxy advances.

So the causal chain is: Proxy reaches signal → SignalBroadcaster detects both sides waiting → releases Twin first via RabbitMQ task queue → Twin's delegate runs → Twin moves past signal → SignalBroadcaster confirms → releases Proxy via RabbitMQ response queue.

When `metaml.messaging.enabled=false`, the same SignalBroadcaster logic runs but calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` directly instead of publishing to RabbitMQ — so the algorithm is identical, just in-process rather than brokered. That's what lets a lone Proxy run to completion with no broker present.

**The `partnerNotComing` fallback** is a counter inside SignalBroadcaster: if after 5 ticks the partner process still hasn't reached the signal, the waiting side gets delivered directly. This lets a lone Proxy complete normally rather than hanging forever.

**Most useful files to start with:**

- `backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — generates all five messaging classes + SignalBroadcaster + PairRegistry + both controllers. The full communication architecture is in here.
- `backend/workbench/src/test/java/com/metaml/workbench/generation/RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest.java` — the acceptance test. Generates a real project, launches it, starts a paired Proxy+Twin, and asserts from both the application log AND the RabbitMQ management API that real messages flowed. This is the strongest existing evidence the synchronization actually works.
- `backend/workbench/src/test/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/LockstepTimingInvariantTest.java` — proves the timing invariant directly: Proxy cannot enter Task N+1 until Twin's Task N has actually completed, not just been signaled. ## Part 2 — How I Can Prove Proxy↔Twin Communication to Joanna

### Evidence classification

**Weak evidence**
- Two terminals showing similar log lines ("Proxy: activity completed" / "Twin: activity completed") with no correlation IDs. This only shows both ran — not that one caused the other.
- Camunda Cockpit showing both process instances are active. Proves they exist, not that they interact.

**Reasonable evidence**
- Log lines showing `TASK: published signal 'X' to RabbitMQ exchange '...' key '...' for execution {executionId}` followed by `TASK: delivered signal 'X' to execution {executionId} via RabbitMQ`. The shared `executionId` strongly suggests causal connection but doesn't independently prove that Proxy was blocked until this happened.
- Showing `RESPONSE: published signal` log followed by `RESPONSE: delivered signal ... via RabbitMQ` with the Proxy's `executionId`. Strong suggestion that Proxy was gated.

**Strong evidence**
Three things together constitute strong proof:
1. **Matching executionId and businessKey across TASK and RESPONSE logs** — proves the same specific instance pair communicated, not just that some messages flowed.
2. **RabbitMQ management API `publish` count > 0 on project-scoped queues** — broker-level evidence independent of the application's own logs. The test at line 167–171 of `RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest` does this exactly.
3. **Camunda engine state showing Proxy did NOT advance until after the RESPONSE was consumed** — this is what `responderHasAdvancedPast()` enforces and what the test asserts at lines 150–153.

The automated test `RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest` asserts all three of these independently and is the strongest existing proof in the repo.

2. Key Technical Concepts:

- **MetaML Workbench**: React + bpmn-js frontend, Spring Boot + Camunda 7.22.0 backend. Pipeline: Model → Generate → Launch → Twin → Govern
- **Two separate synchronization architectures** (critical distinction):
  - **In-process (Workbench)**: AFTER_COMMIT Spring transactional event listener (`AutoBridgeTrigger.java`) — event-driven, no polling, no RabbitMQ
  - **Cross-process (generated Target Platform)**: RabbitMQ + SignalBroadcaster 1-second polling + per-signal queue pairs
- **SignalBroadcaster**: `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)` polls Camunda for executions waiting on signals; for paired Proxy+Twin does a two-step REQUEST→RESPONSE handoff via RabbitMQ; for unpaired delivers directly
- **PairRegistry**: pairs Proxy and Twin process instances by shared `businessKey` — first to register = initiator (proxy), second = responder (twin)
- **RabbitMQ topology**: one DirectExchange per generated project, one task queue + one response queue per shared BPMN signal, all scoped by `messagingNamespace` (projectId-slug) so different generated projects never share queues
- **TaskQueuePublisher / ResponseQueuePublisher**: publish payload `signalName|executionId|processInstanceId|businessKey` to exchange
- **TaskQueueListener / ResponseQueueListener**: `@RabbitListener` consumers; call `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, executionId)` to advance Camunda execution
- **responderHasAdvancedPast()**: checks Twin has truly finished the gated task (no longer subscribed to signalName) before releasing Proxy — proof of lockstep, not just signal arrival
- **`partnerNotComing` fallback**: after 5 polling ticks (~5s) with no partner, delivers signal directly so lone Proxy can still complete
