# Current MetaML Repository Explained

---

## 1. What the system does

MetaML Workbench is a **BPMN-driven process automation platform** with a specific lifecycle: you draw a business process in a visual editor, the Workbench generates a complete standalone Spring Boot application from that drawing, launches it as a real child JVM, and can simultaneously run a **Twin** — a shadow copy of the same process whose activities are executed by pluggable AI agents, gated by a governance policy engine.

The one-line summary from the repo's own README: *"You draw or import a business process, the Workbench generates a complete standalone Spring Boot + Camunda application from it and runs that application as its own JVM, and it can run a Twin of the process whose activities are automated by pluggable agents under a governance layer."*

This is **one working slice of the larger MetaML platform** — specifically Task 1 (process capture + twin + target platform deployment) and Task 3 (governance API). The broader MetaML vision — P2P node networking, Kademlia DHT routing, KMP message protocol — lives in a separate Fall 2025 codebase (`p2p_fall25`) that this team has not touched.

---

## 2. Major components

| Component | Location | Port | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **wbapi** | `backend/wbapi/` | `:8082` | Spring Boot host — REST controllers, Camunda webapp, embeds the `workbench` library |
| **workbench** | `backend/workbench/` | (library) | All domain logic: modeling, twin, generation, governance, bridge, workflow tracking, stores |
| **nodemanager** | `backend/nodemanager/` | `:8083` | Agent catalog stub — properties-file-backed, no real P2P |
| **RedCollarTP** | `backend/RedCollarTP/` | — | Maven archetype/template that generated Target Platform projects are built from |
| **frontend** | `frontend/` | `:3000` | React 19 + bpmn-js 18 UI |
| **Generated Target Platform** | `../generated-target-platforms/{uuid}/` | dynamic | A fully independent Spring Boot + Camunda app, generated and launched at runtime |

---

## 3. End-to-end lifecycle

The complete sequence for one process model:

```
1. Model     → User draws BPMN in frontend (bpmn-js). Saves to backend.
2. Validate  → Camunda validates the BPMN XML at Save time. Failure returns HTTP 400 with element id.
3. Generate  → Backend generates Java delegate stubs + full Spring Boot Target Platform project.
4. Launch    → Backend shells out: mvn clean install → mvn spring-boot:run on the generated project.
               A child JVM starts at a dynamic port. Its activities have REST endpoints.
5. Twin      → User deploys a Twin. The original BPMN is transformed into a Twin BPMN (activity names
               suffixed with "_automate"). Both run in the SAME Camunda engine.
6. Connect   → Each Twin activity is linked to an original activity. The bridge fires automatically.
7. Evolve    → User (or the AutoBridgeTrigger) assigns an agent type to a Twin activity.
               NodeManagerClient checks availability. GovernanceDecisionEngine evaluates tenant policy.
               If ALLOW → agent runs, twin advances. If REQUIRE_APPROVAL → approval goes to queue.
               If DENY → blocked entirely.
8. Govern    → Tenant + platform policies (ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL) evaluated per EVOLVE_TWIN
               action before any agent assignment executes.
```

---

## 4. Workbench architecture

### `backend/workbench/` — the domain library

This module is a pure library (no `main` class, no REST layer). Everything else depends on it.

**Sub-packages and their responsibilities:**

| Package | Key classes | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `service/` | `WorkbenchServiceImpl`, `WorkbenchService` | Central orchestrator — owns all in-memory maps, all cross-cutting workflows |
| `model/` | `ProcessModel`, `TwinProcess`, `BusinessKeys` | Domain records: what a model is, what a twin is, how businessKeys encode identity |
| `store/` | `WorkbenchStateStore`, `ProcessModelFileStore`, `TenantPolicyStore`, `ApprovalStore`, `WorkflowEventStore` | JSON file persistence — atomic writes, rebuilt on restart |
| `bpmn/` | `TwinModelGenerator` | Transforms an original BPMN into a Twin BPMN (adds signal catch events, `_automate` variants, locks) |
| `bridge/` | `AutoBridgeTrigger` | Listens for `AFTER_COMMIT` Camunda `ExecutionEvent` → fires `bridgeActivityEvent()` on the twin |
| `codegen/` | `DelegateClassGenerator`, `TargetPlatformSourceGenerator`, `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator` | Generates Java source: delegate stubs, full Target Platform classes, RabbitMQ messaging infrastructure |
| `generation/` | `SpringBootProjectGenerator`, `SpringBootProjectLauncher`, `BpmnActivities` | Assembles + writes the generated project to disk; shells out `mvn` to build and run it |
| `governance/` | `PolicyDecisionEngine`, `TenantPolicyService`, `ApprovalService`, `TenantPolicyStore` | Full governance implementation: tenant/platform policies, rule evaluation, approval queue |
| `client/` | `NodeManagerClient` | HTTP client that calls nodemanager at `:8083` to check agent availability |
| `workflow/` | `WorkflowStateTracker`, `WorkflowStage`, `StageEvent` | Records the Model→Generate→Launch pipeline history per model, persisted to `WorkflowEventStore` |

### `backend/wbapi/` — the Spring Boot host

Provides the REST layer on top of `workbench`. Key responsibilities:
- Hosts all REST controllers (WorkbenchController, GovernanceController, etc.)
- Embeds the Camunda 7.22.0 engine (`camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter`) with an H2 file-backed database at `data/camunda`
- Configures Spring Security as `permitAll` (localhost-only, no auth by design)
- Registers `AutoBridgeTrigger` as a Spring component — it lives in `workbench` but is activated by the wbapi Spring context

---

## 5. Generated Target Platform

When the user clicks **Generate**, `SpringBootProjectGenerator` does the following:

1. **Reads the BPMN** from the stored model. Uses `TargetPlatformSourceGenerator` to transform delegate expressions into Java-safe class names and generate stub delegate classes (one per BPMN service task).
2. **Detects delegate name collisions** — if two tasks sanitize to the same Java class name, `DelegateClassGenerator` throws `InvalidDelegateExpressionException` carrying the losing element's BPMN id. The frontend uses this id to visually select and highlight the broken element.
3. **Copies RedCollarTP** — the Maven project template — into a new UUID-named directory inside `../generated-target-platforms/` (a sibling of the repo, never committed).
4. **Writes all generated source** into that project: delegate stubs, BPMN file, application.properties. If messaging is enabled, also writes the full RabbitMQ infrastructure (see §8).
5. **When the user clicks Launch**, `SpringBootProjectLauncher` runs `mvn clean install` then `mvn spring-boot:run` as a child process. The generated app starts on a dynamic port and writes a `launch.log`.
6. The generated app is a **fully independent Spring Boot + Camunda application**. It has no classpath dependency on the Workbench. Each BPMN activity that requires external input (user task, receive task, external task) has its own REST endpoint at `POST /{activityId}/complete`.

The generated project is **not** stored in git and not tracked by version control. It lives on disk under `../generated-target-platforms/` and is reconstructed by `SpringBootProjectGenerator.scanExisting()` on Workbench restart. A launched process's JVM does not survive a backend restart — a known limitation documented in the README.

---

## 6. Proxy/Twin architecture

### Conceptual distinction

The words "Proxy" and "Twin" appear in two different contexts in this repo and they mean different things:

**Context A — Workbench in-process (Demo 4 — the Twin workflow):**
- **Original**: the primary Camunda process instance, driven by the user via the Workbench UI.
- **Twin**: a shadow Camunda process instance, running in the same Camunda engine, whose activities are mirrored from the original and automated by agents.
- These run in the **same JVM**, on the **same Camunda engine**, in the **same H2 database**.

**Context B — Generated Target Platform (Demo 5 — the Proxy↔Twin synchronization over RabbitMQ):**
- **Proxy**: one Camunda process instance inside the generated Target Platform, representing the initiator side of a paired synchronization.
- **Twin**: a second Camunda process instance inside the same generated Target Platform, representing the responder side.
- These run in the **same generated JVM** but communicate through **RabbitMQ queues** as if they were cross-process (proving the architecture would work across JVMs).

### How the Workbench Twin works (Context A)

`TwinModelGenerator` transforms the original BPMN into a Twin BPMN by:
- Adding a BPMN signal catch event before each service task (creating a "gate" the original must release).
- Renaming service task delegates to `${activityId_automateTwin}` so both BPMNs can coexist in the same Camunda engine without bean name collisions.

`AutoBridgeTrigger` is the synchronization driver:
- Listens for Camunda `ExecutionEvent` on `AFTER_COMMIT` — fires after the original's transaction commits.
- On each original activity start, calls `workbenchService.bridgeActivityEvent(twinId, activityId, activityInstanceId)`.
- `bridgeActivityEvent()` finds the twin's corresponding activity, checks if it's connected, checks if an agent is assigned, then calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` to release the twin's gate.
- No polling. No RabbitMQ. Pure event-driven in-process Camunda signaling.

**What "Connect", "Evolve", and "Bridge" mean:**
- **Connect**: links a twin activity to an original activity (stores the mapping in `TwinProcess`).
- **Evolve**: assigns an agent type to a connected twin activity. `NodeManagerClient` checks availability; `PolicyDecisionEngine` evaluates tenant policy; if ALLOW, the agent runs and the twin advances.
- **Bridge**: the button that manually triggers `bridgeActivityEvent()` for an activity — what `AutoBridgeTrigger` does automatically.

---

## 7. Synchronization architecture

Two entirely separate synchronization mechanisms exist:

### In-process synchronization (Workbench, Context A)

```
Original commits activity → AFTER_COMMIT ExecutionEvent fires
    → AutoBridgeTrigger.onActivityStarted()
    → executor.submit(runBridge)
    → workbenchService.bridgeActivityEvent()
    → runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, twinExecutionId)
    → Twin's gate releases → Twin's delegate runs synchronously in same transaction
```

**Key properties:**
- Event-driven — no polling, no sleep.
- Same JVM, same Camunda engine, same H2 transaction.
- AFTER_COMMIT ensures the query on the twin's subscription sees committed state.
- Single-threaded executor per `AutoBridgeTrigger` instance — prevents concurrent bridge calls from racing on the same twin.
- No RabbitMQ involved.

### Cross-process synchronization (Generated Target Platform, Context B)

`SignalBroadcaster` (generated class, `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)`) polls Camunda every second:
```
[Tick] SignalBroadcaster polls Camunda for all executions waiting on each shared signal
    → Checks PairRegistry: is this execution a Proxy (initiator) or Twin (responder)?
    → If both Proxy and Twin are waiting on the same signal:
        REQUEST: deliverTo(Twin) → TaskQueuePublisher.publish() → RabbitMQ task queue
            → TaskQueueListener.onTaskMessage() → runtimeService.signalEventReceived(Twin)
            → Twin's delegate runs, Twin advances
        [next tick] responderHasAdvancedPast() confirms Twin is no longer subscribed
        RESPONSE: deliverTo(Proxy) → ResponseQueuePublisher.publish() → RabbitMQ response queue
            → ResponseQueueListener.onResponseMessage() → runtimeService.signalEventReceived(Proxy)
            → Proxy advances
```

**Key properties:**
- Polling (1-second cadence), not event-driven.
- Locks step: Proxy cannot advance until Twin's gated task has COMPLETED (not just been signaled).
- `partnerNotComing` counter: if partner doesn't arrive within ~5 ticks, delivers signal directly so the lone side completes normally.
- When `metaml.messaging.enabled=false`: delivers via `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` directly — identical algorithm, in-process.
- When `metaml.messaging.enabled=true`: delivers through RabbitMQ task/response queues — the brokered, cross-process capable version.

---

## 8. RabbitMQ architecture

**RabbitMQ is NOT part of the Workbench itself.** It lives entirely inside the **generated Target Platform**, and only when `metaml.messaging.enabled=true`.

All RabbitMQ code is **generated, not hand-written**. The generator is `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` (`backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/`). It writes five classes into each generated project's `src/main/java/.../messaging/` package:

| Generated class | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `RabbitMqConfig` | Declares the DirectExchange, one task queue + one response queue per shared BPMN signal, with bindings. Namespace: `{projectId-slug}.sync.{signal-slug}` |
| `TaskQueuePublisher` | Publishes `"signalName\|executionId\|processInstanceId\|businessKey"` to the task queue (Proxy side has reached a shared signal) |
| `TaskQueueListener` | `@RabbitListener` — consumes task queue, calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, twinExecutionId)` |
| `ResponseQueuePublisher` | Publishes the same payload to the response queue (Twin has completed) |
| `ResponseQueueListener` | `@RabbitListener` — consumes response queue, calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, proxyExecutionId)` |

The generator also produces `SignalBroadcaster`, `PairRegistry`, `ProxyProcessController`, and `TwinProcessController` into sibling packages.

Queue naming is namespaced per generated project using the `messagingNamespace` (projectId slug), so two independently generated Target Platforms on the same RabbitMQ broker never share queues, even if their BPMNs have identically-named signals.

---

## 9. Governance

Governance is **fully implemented** — not a stub. It covers three distinct layers:

### Tenant/policy model

- **Tenant**: a named group (created via the Governance UI).
- **Policy**: scoped to either a tenant or the platform (null tenantId = platform-wide).
- **PolicyVersion**: draft/active lifecycle — only active versions are evaluated.
- **PolicyRule**: a single `field operator value` expression (e.g. `action == EVOLVE_TWIN`, `riskFlagged == true`). Operators: `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`.
- **PolicyEffect**: `ALLOW`, `DENY`, `REQUIRE_APPROVAL`.

All of this persists to JSON files under `backend/wbapi/data/`.

### PolicyDecisionEngine

`PolicyDecisionEngine.evaluate(GovernanceRequest)` is called before every agent assignment:
1. Checks both platform policies and the tenant's own policies.
2. Picks the most severe matching rule (DENY > REQUIRE_APPROVAL > ALLOW). Platform wins on ties.
3. If no rule matches: default `ALLOW` (silence is not a block).
4. Returns a `PolicyDecision` record with the matched rule, version, and policy id for audit.

`GovernanceRequest` carries: `tenantId`, `action` (always `"EVOLVE_TWIN"` for evolve), `attributes` (arbitrary key-value pairs the rule can match against, e.g. `riskFlagged=true`).

### Approval queue

When the decision is `REQUIRE_APPROVAL`:
- `ApprovalService` creates an `Approval` record (persisted to `ApprovalStore`).
- The twin activity is NOT advanced — it waits.
- A human reviewer visits the Governance → Approvals UI and either approves or rejects.
- On approve: the evolution runs, the twin advances. On reject: nothing runs.

**The audit trail** (which policy, which version, which rule matched) is stored on every `PolicyDecision`, not just the final outcome.

### Tenant ownership

Each model can be assigned a `tenantId` at creation time (via the Transmute → Create Project UI). That tenantId flows through to every `TwinProcess` and every `GovernanceRequest` at evolve time, so tenant isolation is enforced at the call site, not inferred.

**Known limitation:** `tenantId` is caller-supplied and never authenticated — documented explicitly in the README and every governance UI label.

---

## 10. Node Manager

**Status: Stub implementation.**

`nodemanager` is a standalone Spring Boot app at `:8083` that simulates an AI agent catalog lookup. Its only real implementation is:
- Read `application.yml` for a named list of agent types and their declared outputs.
- `POST /agents/{agentType}/availability` → returns `AgentAvailabilityResponse` (available: true/false, agentName, outputs map).

The "catalog" currently has five entries: `data-enricher`, `notifier`, `validator`, `recommender`, and `credit-risk-assessor`. The last one is the only entry that returns any actual output values (`riskFlagged: true`) — the rest only report that they exist.

`NodeManagerClient` in `workbench` calls this endpoint over HTTP before every evolve. If the nodemanager is unreachable, `NodeManagerUnavailableException` is thrown and the evolve fails with a clear message.

**There is no real AI or P2P integration here.** The real MetaML P2P node manager (`p2p_fall25`) is a separate codebase this team has not integrated with. The stub exists to prove the client-side integration path (HTTP availability check → governance → evolve) works end to end.

---

## 11. Frontend

React 19, Create React App, `bpmn-js` 18. No automated tests beyond CRA baseline.

**Pages:**

| Page | Menu | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ModelPage.js` | Transmute → Create Project | The main working surface. bpmn-js editor + BPMN import/export + Save/Generate/Launch/Stop workflow breadcrumb with status colors. "Go to error" highlights a failing element in the editor. |
| `EditProjectListPage.js` | Transmute → Edit Existing Project | Lists saved models, opens one in ModelPage. |
| `GenerateProjectListPage.js` | Transmute | Shows generation status per model. |
| `LaunchProjectListPage.js` | Transmute | Shows launch status + Stop button. |

| `EvolvePage.js` | Evolve → Twin Workflow | The twin control surface: Connect/Evolve/Bridge buttons per activity, shows agent assignment, governance decisions. |
| `GovernancePoliciesPage.js` | Governance → Policies | Create tenants, draft/activate policies, add rules. |
| `GovernanceApprovalsPage.js` | Governance → Approvals | Review and resolve pending approvals. |

The BPMN file import in `ModelPage` **only validates that `bpmn-js` can parse the XML** — it does not deploy or save. The first Camunda validation happens at Save. This is explicitly documented in the README ("What not to claim about it" section).

## 12. Tests and what they prove

### Core unit/integration tests (no RabbitMQ, no external process)

| Test class | What it proves |
|---|---|
| `LockstepTimingInvariantTest` | **The timing invariant**: Proxy cannot enter Task N+1 until Twin's Task N delegate has COMPLETED — proved via Camunda's own history timestamps, not test-thread clocks. Uses CountDownLatch to hold Twin's delegate in-flight while asserting Proxy is still blocked. No RabbitMQ, no SignalBroadcaster. |
| `LockstepSyncIntegrationTest` | The SHAPE of the generated BPMN (signal gates exist in the right places). Does not run a real engine. |
| `DelegateClassGeneratorTest` | Delegate class name collision detection (14 tests). Verifies the right element id is blamed. |
| `SpringBootProjectGeneratorTest` | Generated project structure is correct — right files, right packages, right pom.xml content. |
| `SpringBootProjectLauncherTest` | Launcher's liveness registry correctly rejects dead processes (the `isAlive()` fix). |
| `WireTransferWalkthroughTest` | Full end-to-end walkthrough in the wbapi Spring context: model → generate → twin → connect → evolve → governance. |

### Slow tests (real Maven builds, real JVMs, real RabbitMQ)

| Test class | What it proves |
|---|---|
| `RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest` | Generates a real Target Platform from real BPMNs, launches it, starts Proxy+Twin with same businessKey, then asserts: (1) launch.log contains "published signal ... to RabbitMQ exchange", (2) RabbitMQ management API shows publish count > 0 on project-scoped queues, (3) Camunda engine state shows both instances advanced. Three independent evidence sources — the strongest available proof of end-to-end Proxy↔Twin synchronization. |
| `SpringBootProjectLauncherMavenInstallTest` | Verifies the launcher can shell out to `mvn`. Fails in the current environment (no system-wide `mvn`) — the 1 known failing test. |

**Total: 299 tests, 1 failure** (environment-dependent). 17 additional `@Tag("slow")` tests excluded from default runs.

## 13. What is implemented vs incomplete

### Fully implemented and tested

- BPMN model capture, validation, save (with element-level error recovery for delegate collisions)
- Target Platform generation from any BPMN (delegate stubs, Spring Boot project, launch/stop lifecycle)
- Full governance pipeline: tenant → policy → version → rule → `PolicyDecisionEngine` → ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL → approval queue
- In-process Original↔Twin synchronization via `AutoBridgeTrigger` (AFTER_COMMIT, no polling)
- Proxy↔Twin cross-process synchronization via `SignalBroadcaster` + RabbitMQ queues (generated code)
- `PairRegistry` / lockstep timing invariant (proved by `LockstepTimingInvariantTest`)
- File-backed persistence for models, twins, governance, approvals, workflow history — all survive backend restart
- Generated project restart persistence (reconstructed from disk on startup, not from a new store)
- Liveness tracking — dead child JVMs are detected via `Process.isAlive()` and removed from registry

### Stub / incomplete

- **Node Manager**: catalog is a static `application.yml` with 5 hardcoded agent types. No real AI, no real P2P integration. The `credit-risk-assessor` is the only one that returns any meaningful output.
- **RabbitMQ in the Workbench itself**: zero. RabbitMQ only exists in the generated Target Platform.
- **Authentication**: none. `tenantId` is caller-supplied, `permitAll` everywhere. Documented as deliberate demo scope.
- **Generated project cleanup**: no deletion mechanism. Directories accumulate on disk indefinitely.
- **Launch log in the UI**: the log path is surfaced on failure but the content is not inlined.
- **Multi-tenant authentication**: tenant isolation is scoping, not enforcement — a caller can supply any tenant id.
- **Governance quota persistence**: platform evolution quota resets to defaults on backend restart (in-memory only).
- **Real P2P integration**: the `p2p_fall25` codebase (Kademlia DHT, KMP protocol) is a separate project this team has not integrated with.

### What the README covers well

- Prerequisites, run commands, known limitations, what not to claim — all accurate and up to date.
- Repository layout at the directory level.
- The five demo scenarios and what each demonstrates.

### What the README does not cover

- The internal architecture of each module (who calls whom, what the service layer does).
- The distinction between in-process synchronization (AutoBridgeTrigger) and generated cross-process synchronization (SignalBroadcaster + RabbitMQ).
- The fact that RabbitMQ code is entirely generated — not a Workbench dependency.
- The governance data model (Tenant → Policy → Version → Rule → PolicyDecisionEngine evaluation flow).
- The Node Manager stub limitation (static YAML, no real AI or P2P).
- The "Proxy" and "Twin" terminology appearing in two different contexts with different meanings.
- The `PLATFORM_CONTEXT.md` (which is the best document for understanding what this team owns vs what predates them) is not mentioned prominently in the README.

## Part 1 — Email to Joanna

Hi Joanna,

I wanted to give you a clear picture of where everything lives in the repository, since you mentioned wanting to look at the code directly.

**Repository structure**

The backend splits into three separate Spring Boot modules:
- `backend/workbench/` — all domain logic: BPMN modeling, code generation, twin architecture, governance, bridge. No REST layer, no main class. Everything else depends on this as a library.
- `backend/wbapi/` — the Spring Boot host that runs at `:8082`. Provides the REST API and embeds Camunda 7.22.0.
- `backend/nodemanager/` — an agent catalog stub at `:8083`. Five hardcoded agent types in `application.yml`. No real AI or P2P behind it.

**What the system actually does**

You draw a BPMN process in the frontend, save it, and the Workbench generates a complete standalone Spring Boot + Camunda project from that drawing — then launches it as its own child JVM. The main source file to understand that generation is `backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/generation/SpringBootProjectGenerator.java`. The generated project lands in a `../generated-target-platforms/{uuid}/` directory outside the repo.

Separately, the Workbench can deploy a **Twin** of any process — a shadow Camunda process instance running in the same engine whose activities are automated by agents (the Node Manager integration) and gated by a governance policy engine (the full ALLOW/DENY/REQUIRE_APPROVAL implementation in `backend/workbench/.../governance/`).

**RabbitMQ — where it is and what it does**

RabbitMQ does not live in the Workbench. The Workbench's own Original↔Twin synchronization is purely event-driven: `backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/bridge/AutoBridgeTrigger.java` listens for a Spring `AFTER_COMMIT` event after each original process activity commits, then calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` to release the corresponding twin gate. No polling, no broker.

RabbitMQ lives entirely inside the **generated Target Platform** — the separate Spring Boot app that gets synthesized when you run the Proxy↔Twin scenario. All of it is code that gets written by `backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` into the generated project. The generator produces five classes: `RabbitMqConfig`, `TaskQueuePublisher`, `TaskQueueListener`, `ResponseQueuePublisher`, and `ResponseQueueListener`. None of these are hand-written; they're string templates instantiated per project.

**Proxy↔Twin communication in the generated platform**

The synchronization driver is `SignalBroadcaster` (also generated), which polls Camunda every second for executions waiting on shared BPMN signals. When it detects both a Proxy and a Twin waiting on the same signal:

1. It releases the Twin first by publishing to the RabbitMQ task queue (`TaskQueuePublisher.publish()`).
2. `TaskQueueListener` consumes that message and calls `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` on the Twin's execution — Twin's delegate runs synchronously inside that Camunda transaction.
3. SignalBroadcaster then waits for confirmation that the Twin actually advanced (using `responderHasAdvancedPast()`, which re-queries Camunda to verify Twin is no longer subscribed to the signal). This is the lockstep guarantee: the Proxy cannot move until the Twin's task has completed, not just been signaled.
4. Only then does it release the Proxy, by publishing to the response queue. `ResponseQueueListener` consumes it and releases the Proxy's execution.

The Proxy and Twin pair up using a shared `businessKey` supplied at startup via `/api/proxy/start?businessKey=X` and `/api/twin/start?businessKey=X`. The first to register becomes the initiator; the second becomes the responder. `PairRegistry` (also generated) holds this mapping.

**Most useful starting files:**
- `backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — the generator that produces all RabbitMQ infrastructure
- `backend/workbench/src/test/java/com/metaml/workbench/generation/RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest.java` — the acceptance test. Generates a real project, launches it, starts a paired Proxy+Twin, and asserts from both the application log AND the RabbitMQ management API that real messages flowed.
- `backend/workbench/src/test/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/LockstepTimingInvariantTest.java` — proves the timing invariant directly: Proxy cannot enter Task N+1 until Twin's Task N has COMPLETED, using Camunda's own recorded history timestamps as the clock.

Let me know if you'd like a walkthrough of any specific piece.

Nirman

## Part 2 — How I Can Prove Proxy↔Twin Communication to Joanna

### Evidence tiers

**Weak**
- Two terminals showing process activity logs with similar timestamps. Shows both ran, not that one caused the other.
- Camunda Cockpit showing both process instances exist. Proves existence, not interaction.

**Reasonable**
- Log lines showing `TASK: published signal ... to RabbitMQ exchange` + `TASK: delivered signal ... via RabbitMQ` with matching `executionId`. The shared id strongly suggests causality but doesn't independently prove that the Proxy was blocked while waiting.
- `RESPONSE: published signal` + `RESPONSE: delivered signal ... via RabbitMQ` with the Proxy's `processInstanceId`. Strong suggestion the Proxy was gated, but still log-text only.

**Strong — three independent sources, all must agree:**
1. **Application log**: matching `executionId` and `businessKey` across TASK and RESPONSE phases.
2. **RabbitMQ management API** (`http://localhost:15672/api/queues/%2f`): publish count > 0 on project-scoped queues — broker-level evidence independent of the application's own log. The acceptance test asserts this at lines 167–171.
3. **Camunda engine state**: `responderHasAdvancedPast()` confirms the Twin advanced before the Proxy was released. Equivalently: Proxy's history shows it entered its next activity only *after* Twin's history shows Twin's gated task completed. The acceptance test asserts this at lines 150–153.

`LockstepTimingInvariantTest` provides a fourth source: Camunda's own `HistoricActivityInstance.endTime` for Twin's delegate is `beforeOrEqualTo` `startTime` for Proxy's next activity — engine-recorded timestamps, not test clocks or log text.

---

### Live demonstration steps

**Setup**
```powershell
# Terminal 1 — RabbitMQ
docker run -d -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:3-management

# Terminal 2 — Workbench backend (already running during the demo)
cd backend; .\mvnw.cmd -pl wbapi spring-boot:run

# Terminal 3 — Frontend
cd frontend; npm start
```

Use the Workbench UI to Generate and Launch the Manuf/Twin scenario from `demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn` + `demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn`. Alternatively, use an already-generated project in `wbapi/data/generated-projects/`. In either case, the generated project must be started with `--metaml.messaging.enabled=true`.

**Step 1 — Start Proxy**
```powershell
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/proxy/start?businessKey=demo1"
```
Note the `processInstanceId` returned. Confirm `"role":"initiator"` in the JSON.

**Step 2 — Start Twin**
```powershell
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/twin/start?businessKey=demo1"
```
Note the `processInstanceId`. Confirm `"role":"responder"`.

**Step 3 — Show the REQUEST phase in the log**

Within ~2 seconds in the generated app's terminal:
```
TASK: published signal 'orderReadySignal' to RabbitMQ exchange '...' key '...' for execution {twinExecutionId} (processInstanceId={twinId}, businessKey=demo1)
TASK: delivered signal 'orderReadySignal' to execution {twinExecutionId} via RabbitMQ
```
Point out: `businessKey=demo1` matches what was supplied. The Twin's `executionId` appears here — the Proxy's does not. SignalBroadcaster detected both sides waiting and released the Twin first.

**Step 4 — Show the RESPONSE phase**
```
RESPONSE: published signal 'orderReadySignal' to RabbitMQ exchange '...' key '...' for execution {proxyExecutionId} (processInstanceId={proxyId}, businessKey=demo1)
RESPONSE: delivered signal 'orderReadySignal' to execution {proxyExecutionId} via RabbitMQ
```
Now the Proxy's `executionId` appears. Point out: Proxy was held until this line. The log shows a gap between the TASK delivery and the RESPONSE delivery — that gap is `responderHasAdvancedPast()` confirming the Twin's transaction committed.

**Step 5 — Show the RabbitMQ management UI**

Open `http://localhost:15672/#/queues`. Show queues named `{projectId}.sync.{signal-slug}` and `{projectId}.sync.responses.{signal-slug}` with `publish` counts > 0. This is broker-level evidence with no reliance on application logging.

**Code files to have open alongside**

| If Joanna asks | File to open |
|---|---|
| "Where is SignalBroadcaster?" | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — the `signalBroadcaster()` method |
| "Where does it publish to RabbitMQ?" | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — `TaskQueuePublisher.publish()` method template |
| "Where does the Twin advance?" | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — `TaskQueueListener.onTaskMessage()` template — `runtimeService.signalEventReceived()` |
| "How does it know the Proxy can advance?" | `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java` — `responderHasAdvancedPast()` template |
| "Does a test prove this?" | `RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest.java` lines 135–173 |

### Best Proof Demo

**Run the acceptance test with RabbitMQ running:**

```powershell
cd backend
.\mvnw.cmd -pl workbench test -Dtest=RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest -Dgroups=slow
```

This is the strongest single proof because it asserts four independent facts automatically:
1. Log contains `"TASK: published signal ... to RabbitMQ exchange"` — publisher ran.
2. Log contains `"delivered signal ... via RabbitMQ"` — listener consumed and delivered.
3. **RabbitMQ management API returns publish count > 0** on project-scoped queues — broker-level confirmation, independent of log text.
4. Camunda engine state shows both instances advanced — not just that messages were sent.

Any one of these failing makes the entire test fail. Passing all four simultaneously is causal proof, not correlation. The test produces no false positives: if the queues exist but nothing was published, assertion 3 fails; if the log claims delivery but the engine didn't advance, assertion 4 fails.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 6:28:54 PM</sup>

Hi Joanna,

I wanted to point you to the main places in the updated repo where the Proxy/Twin communication and RabbitMQ pieces are implemented, so you can follow the flow directly in the code.

At a high level, the backend is split into three main pieces under `backend/`: `workbench`, which contains the core BPMN, generation, runtime, and governance logic; `wbapi`, which provides the Spring Boot/Camunda host and API layer; and `nodemanager`, which is currently a lightweight agent catalog. There is also `backend/RedCollarTP`, which serves as the generated Target Platform template for the Proxy/Twin setup.

The important distinction: RabbitMQ does not drive the Workbench's internal Original/Twin synchronization. That synchronization is event-driven — `AutoBridgeTrigger.java` fires after each original activity commits and advances the twin in-process, with no broker involved. RabbitMQ comes into play in the generated Target Platform, where it provides the communication mechanism between the separately running Proxy and Twin sides.

The main code that generates this communication layer is:

`backend/workbench/src/main/java/com/metaml/workbench/codegen/TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java`

That generator creates the RabbitMQ configuration, publishers, and listeners in the generated Target Platform. The task queue is used to release the Twin, while the response queue is used to release the Proxy. The listeners ultimately call Camunda's `runtimeService.signalEventReceived(...)` to advance the corresponding execution.

The Proxy/Twin coordination itself is handled by the generated `PairRegistry` and `SignalBroadcaster`. The two sides pair using the same business key, and `SignalBroadcaster` coordinates which side advances first. In the normal paired flow, the Twin is released first, its task completes, and only after the Twin has moved past the synchronization point does the Proxy receive the corresponding response and continue.

So the flow is:

Proxy/Twin reach synchronization point → SignalBroadcaster detects the pair → RabbitMQ task message releases Twin → Twin completes its activity → Twin's progress is confirmed → RabbitMQ response releases Proxy → Proxy continues.

If messaging is disabled, the same synchronization logic delivers the Camunda signal directly in-process instead of going through RabbitMQ. That distinction is useful when reading the code because the synchronization algorithm and the transport mechanism are kept separate.

The two tests I'd particularly point you toward are:

- `RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest.java`, which exercises an actual generated Proxy/Twin setup and verifies the RabbitMQ communication end to end.
- `LockstepTimingInvariantTest.java`, which specifically verifies that the Proxy does not move ahead until the Twin has actually completed its corresponding step.

If you're looking at the repo to understand the communication, I'd start with `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.java`, then follow the generated `SignalBroadcaster`, `PairRegistry`, the RabbitMQ publishers/listeners, and finally the end-to-end synchronization test. That gives you the architecture, the actual implementation, and the proof that the two sides work together.

Nirman

**Prerequisites — get these running first**

```powershell

```

Then use the Workbench to Generate + Launch the `demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn` / `demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn` pair. The generated app starts at a dynamic port — check the Workbench UI or `launch.log` for the exact port. Replace `8080` below with whatever it shows.

---

**Terminal 1 — watch the generated app's output live**

Keep the terminal where the generated app launched open. That's where the TASK/RESPONSE lines appear in real time.

---

**Terminal 2 — start the Proxy, then the Twin**

```powershell
# Start Proxy
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/proxy/start?businessKey=joanna-demo"
```

```powershell
# Start Twin (run immediately after — same businessKey)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/twin/start?businessKey=joanna-demo"
```

Watch Terminal 1 — within ~2 seconds you'll see the TASK then RESPONSE log lines with `businessKey=joanna-demo`.

---

**Terminal 3 — broker-level proof from the RabbitMQ management API**

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod `
  -Uri "http://localhost:15672/api/queues/%2f" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Basic " + [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("guest:guest")) } |
  Where-Object { $_.name -like "*sync*" } |
  Select-Object name, @{n="published";e={$_.message_stats.publish}}
```

This hits the broker directly — no application logs involved. You should see your two queues (`...sync...` and `...sync.responses...`) both showing `published` > 0. That's the screenshot to take.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 6:45:34 PM</sup>

That's the proof. The Twin ran all its activities sequentially — every `**** TWIN - ...Twin ---- Spring Bean invoked` line is a generated delegate executing inside the Twin's Camunda process.

But I don't see the RabbitMQ TASK/RESPONSE lines, which means `messaging.enabled=true` may not have been picked up. Check with:

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod "http://localhost:15672/api/queues/%2f" -Headers @{ Authorization = "Basic " + [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("guest:guest")) } | Where-Object { $_.name -like "*sync*" } | Select-Object name, @{n="published";e={$_.message_stats.publish}}
```

If that returns nothing, the messaging flag didn't take effect and signals were delivered in-process (the `DELIVERED:` line confirms delivery happened — just not through RabbitMQ). 

To force RabbitMQ, stop the generated app and recheck — the startup log should have a line like `metaml.messaging.enabled: true`. Did you see that during startup?

# editor - a BPMN authored there has no reason to already carry that attribute. Disabling enforcement
# here, once, for every generated Target Platform is what actually matches that workflow; requiring
# every user-drawn proxy/twin BPMN to remember a Camunda-specific attribute would not.

# RabbitListener beans it activates simply have nothing to bind if there are no shared signals.

# Retries connecting rather than failing startup outright if the broker isn't up yet when this

spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.retry.enabled=true

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 6:58:01 PM</sup>

Confirms it: the old instance (from earlier, PID 32848) is still running on port 8080 — since Ctrl+C never worked, it never actually stopped. That's also why RabbitMQ properties looked like they weren't taking effect — you were still hitting the OLD process the whole time.

Kill it:

```powershell
Get-Process -Name java | Stop-Process -Force
```

Then restart:

```powershell
mvn clean spring-boot:run 2>&1 | Tee-Object -FilePath "startup.log"
```

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 7:00:59 PM</sup>

Found it — this is the real issue, not a config problem.

Look at `RabbitMqConfig.java`: `TASK_QUEUE_BY_SIGNAL` and the other three maps are **empty** (`Map.ofEntries()` with nothing inside). That means the generator found **zero shared signals** between this particular Proxy and Twin BPMN pair — so no queues were ever created, and every signal (including `sync_taste_check`) gets delivered **directly in-process** instead of through RabbitMQ. That matches exactly what you saw: the Twin ran through all its steps instantly with no RabbitMQ activity.

This project (`ee4648f2...`) looks like it was generated from a cooking/rice-prep BPMN (`prepareingredients`, `heatwok`, `scrambleeggs`...) — not the `demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn` + `demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn` pair the README and the acceptance test actually use for the RabbitMQ demo. That pair is specifically built with multiple shared signals so the queues get populated.

**Fix:** regenerate using the correct demo fixtures.

1. In the Workbench UI, load **`demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn`** as the base model, save it.
2. Deploy its Twin from **`demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn`**.
3. Generate + Launch that pair — a new UUID folder appears in `generated-target-platforms/`.
4. Set `metaml.messaging.enabled=true` in that new project's `application.properties` (it may already default to true, like this one did).
5. Repeat the Proxy/Twin start + RabbitMQ check against the new UUID.

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 7:01:39 PM</sup>

Found the actual root cause. Look at the two BPMNs:

- **`Process_1.bpmn` (Proxy)** — has 7 signal catch events (`sync_prepareingredients`, `sync_heatwok`, ... `sync_taste_check`). It's designed to pause and wait at each one.
- **`Process_1_twin.bpmn` (Twin)** — has **zero signal events**. It's just a plain straight-through sequence: prep → heat wok → scramble eggs → ... → end. Nothing in it ever throws or catches any of those signals.

So this Proxy/Twin pair isn't actually built to synchronize with each other. The generator only creates a RabbitMQ queue for a signal when **both sides reference it** — since the Twin never references any of the Proxy's signals, `TASK_QUEUE_BY_SIGNAL` stays empty (correctly, per the generator's own logic), and every signal on the Proxy side falls into the "only one side has it" case — delivered directly in-process, no broker involved. That's exactly what you saw: Twin ran straight through instantly, no RabbitMQ activity, no queues.

**This isn't fixable by restarting or reconfiguring** — the BPMN pair itself doesn't have shared sync points. To see the RabbitMQ flow, you need a Twin BPMN that was actually generated/authored to share signal events with the Proxy, like `demo/Manuf-camunda.bpmn` + `demo/Twin-camunda.bpmn` — the pair the README and the acceptance test specifically use for this demo.

Want to switch to those two files and regenerate, or do you want to first check how this fried-rice Twin BPMN got generated without any sync signals (maybe it wasn't created via "Deploy Twin" the way `Twin-camunda.bpmn` was)?

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 7:09:06 PM</sup>

This is it — look for the key line:

```
o.s.a.r.c.CachingConnectionFactory : Attempting to connect to: [localhost:5672]
o.s.a.r.c.CachingConnectionFactory : Created new connection: rabbitConnectionFactory#...
```

The app actually connected to RabbitMQ this time. Now start Proxy and Twin:

**Terminal — Proxy**
```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Method POST "http://localhost:8080/api/proxy/start?businessKey=demo4"
```

**Terminal — Twin**
```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Method POST "http://localhost:8080/api/twin/start?businessKey=demo4"
```

Then paste what appears in the app terminal, and run the RabbitMQ check:

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod "http://localhost:15672/api/queues/%2f" -Headers @{ Authorization = "Basic " + [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("guest:guest")) } | Where-Object { $_.name -like "*sync*" } | Select-Object name, @{n="published";e={$_.message_stats.publish}}
```

## Assistant <sup>8/26/2026, 7:10:22 PM</sup>

That's expected — you only started the Proxy. It's now parked waiting for its Twin partner to show up on the same businessKey before `SignalBroadcaster` does anything. Start the Twin now:

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Method POST "http://localhost:8080/api/twin/start?businessKey=demo4"
```

Then watch the app terminal — within ~2 seconds you should see `TASK: published signal ... to RabbitMQ exchange`. Paste what appears.

## Traced through the current code

**1. Which component publishes to each queue**

`sync.{signal}` (task queues) and `sync.responses.{signal}` (response queues) are both declared in `RabbitMqConfig` — generated by `TargetPlatformMessagingGenerator.messaging()`. Publishing to them happens in exactly two classes:

- `TaskQueuePublisher.publish()` → publishes to `sync.{signal}` (routing key `sync.{signal-slug}`)
- `ResponseQueuePublisher.publish()` → publishes to `sync.responses.{signal}` (routing key `sync.responses.{signal-slug}`)

Both are only ever called from one place: `SignalBroadcaster.deliverTo()`, at the `@Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000)` poll in `broadcastSignals()`.

**2. Do `sync.*` queues represent Proxy → Twin?**

Yes, specifically. Look at `SignalBroadcaster.handle()`: the `"REQUEST"` phase is only ever triggered when the current subscription being examined is the **initiator's** (Proxy's), and it calls `deliverTo(signalName, responderSubscription, ..., "REQUEST")` — note it passes the **responder's (Twin's) subscription**, not its own. `deliverTo()` then routes `"REQUEST"` phase to `taskQueuePublisher.publish(signalName, subscription.getExecutionId(), ...)` using that Twin subscription's executionId. So: **the Proxy side of the broadcaster logic triggers the publish, but the payload identifies the Twin's execution** — the task queue is the mechanism that releases the Twin.

**3. Do `sync.responses.*` queues represent Twin → Proxy?**

Yes. The `"RESPONSE"` phase only fires after `responderHasAdvancedPast()` confirms the Twin's gated task actually completed (checked via `awaitingResponse.contains(handoffKey)` + a subsequent poll tick). When that's true, `deliverTo(signalName, subscription, ..., "RESPONSE")` is called with **the Proxy's own subscription** — this is the call inside the branch where `subscription` is literally the Proxy's own execution being examined that tick. So the response queue payload identifies the Proxy's execution — its purpose is releasing the Proxy.

**4. Which generated classes publish**

`TaskQueuePublisher` and `ResponseQueuePublisher` — both `@Component`, both wrap `RabbitTemplate.convertAndSend()`, called only by `SignalBroadcaster`.

**5. Which generated classes consume**

`TaskQueueListener.onTaskMessage()` (`@RabbitListener` on the task queues) and `ResponseQueueListener.onResponseMessage()` (`@RabbitListener` on the response queues).

**6/7. What happens after each listener receives a message — does it call `signalEventReceived`?**

Yes, both do, directly:
```java
runtimeService.signalEventReceived(signalName, executionId);
```
`executionId` is parsed straight out of the pipe-delimited payload (`signalName|executionId|processInstanceId|businessKey`) — not looked up, not re-derived. Whatever `TaskQueuePublisher`/`ResponseQueuePublisher` put in the payload is exactly what gets signaled.

**8. Which execution is released on which side**

- `TaskQueueListener` releases the **Twin's** execution (because the payload it consumes was published with the Twin's executionId, per point 2).
- `ResponseQueueListener` releases the **Proxy's** execution (payload published with the Proxy's executionId, per point 3).

**9. Can businessKey / processInstanceId / executionId correlate the two sides?**

Yes — all three travel together in the payload and appear together in every log line (`TASK: published signal ... for execution {id} (processInstanceId={id}, businessKey={key})`). Since both `/proxy/start` and `/twin/start` are called with the same `businessKey`, and `PairRegistry` pairs them by that key, you can trace: businessKey → which two processInstanceIds were paired → which executionId was named in the TASK payload vs. the RESPONSE payload. That's a full audit trail.

**10. Does `published: 1` come from RabbitMQ itself, or from app-level logging/inspection?**

**From RabbitMQ itself.** `http://localhost:15672/api/queues/%2f` is the RabbitMQ management HTTP API — it reports `message_stats.publish` from the broker's own internal counters, independent of anything the generated app logs. This is broker-side telemetry, not a reflection of application log text.

## Does the actual code match your assumed flow diagram?

Your diagram is **correct**, with one refinement: "Twin completion confirmed" isn't a separate message — it's `SignalBroadcaster.responderHasAdvancedPast()` polling Camunda's own event-subscription state on a *later broadcaster tick* (no new RabbitMQ message for this step). So:

```
Proxy reaches signal, Twin already waiting on it (same signal, same businessKey pair)
    ↓
SignalBroadcaster (1s poll) detects the pair, phase=REQUEST
    ↓
TaskQueuePublisher.publish() → sync.{signal} queue → RabbitMQ
    ↓
TaskQueueListener.onTaskMessage() consumes → runtimeService.signalEventReceived(Twin's executionId)
    ↓
Twin's gated delegate runs synchronously, Twin's execution moves off that signal
    ↓
[NOT a RabbitMQ message] — next broadcaster tick, responderHasAdvancedPast() re-queries Camunda,
    confirms Twin's execution is no longer subscribed to that signal name
    ↓
SignalBroadcaster phase=RESPONSE
    ↓
ResponseQueuePublisher.publish() → sync.responses.{signal} queue → RabbitMQ
    ↓
ResponseQueueListener.onResponseMessage() consumes → runtimeService.signalEventReceived(Proxy's executionId)
    ↓
Proxy's execution advances
```

Your diagram is right in substance; the one correction is that "Twin completion confirmed" is a **Camunda query on the broadcaster's own next tick**, not a RabbitMQ event.

## What the Code Shows About the Debugging/Fixes

**Issue → RESPONDER STARTS AFTER ITS INITIATOR ALREADY PASSED THE SIGNAL (race condition #1)**
- **Fix in code:** `everDelivered` set + `partnerNotComing()` fallback in `SignalBroadcaster`
- **Evidence:** commit `4ffb6d8` message states directly: *"a responder starting after its initiator had already passed a signal alone could wait forever."* The `everDelivered` field comment explains exactly this scenario: "a rework-loop revisit, or the partner's earlier unpaired delivery before the other side ever registered." The diff shows this being added, not present from the start.
- **Why it matters:** without it, a Twin that starts even slightly late relative to its Proxy would be waiting on a signal the Proxy has already moved past — with nothing ever arriving to release it. This is a genuine startup-ordering race, not defensive boilerplate.

**Issue → A SIGNAL DECLARED ON ONLY ONE SIDE'S BPMN NEVER HAS A REAL CO-WAITING PARTNER (structural deadlock)**
- **Fix in code:** `partnerArrivalTicks` + `MAX_PARTNER_ARRIVAL_TICKS = 5` bound in `SignalBroadcaster`
- **Evidence:** same commit `4ffb6d8`: *"a signal that exists in only one side's BPMN (e.g. RedCollar's own Manuf-only orderVerifySignal) had a registered partner that would structurally never co-wait on it, also waiting forever."* The field comment on `partnerArrivalTicks` states this explicitly as the reason a bound is needed at all.
- **Why it matters:** `orderVerifySignal` is a real signal in the actual RedCollar BPMN the professor supplied — this isn't hypothetical. Without the tick bound, that execution hangs forever with no automatic recovery.

**Issue → RABBITMQ NOT UP YET WHEN THE GENERATED APP LAUNCHES (startup ordering/readiness)**
- **Fix in code:** `spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.retry.enabled=true`, `initial-interval=2000`, `max-attempts=30` in the generated `application.properties` template
- **Evidence:** commit `30d8156` message: *"RedCollarTP: metaml.messaging.enabled=true by default, with retrying RabbitMQ listener startup so a broker that isn't up the instant this process launches doesn't fail startup outright."* The inline comment in the properties file goes further, distinguishing this from a compile failure: *"a slower, noisier failure ... is preferable to a fast one that then reads as 'the generated project itself is broken' to SpringBootProjectLauncher.awaitReady, which was written to diagnose a COMPILE failure, not this."*
- **Why it matters:** this is a direct admission that without the retry config, a slow-starting broker was previously misdiagnosed by the launcher as a broken generated project — a real debugging dead-end that got fixed by adding retry semantics, not just a defensive default.

**Issue → PROXY RELEASED BEFORE THE TWIN'S GATED TASK ACTUALLY COMPLETED (lockstep violation)**
- **Fix in code:** `awaitingResponse` set + `responderHasAdvancedPast()` re-query
- **Evidence:** the method's own doc comment is explicit about what it's guarding against: *"proof that the gated task actually finished, rather than merely that it started. A delegate that hands work to another thread and returns early would make this method return true before the real work is done."* `LockstepTimingInvariantTest.java` (added in commit `d58aea3`, a dedicated 278-line test file) exists specifically to assert this invariant with a `CountDownLatch`-blocked delegate, proving the Proxy stays blocked on `sync_evt_taskA` while the Twin's delegate is provably still running.
- **Why it matters:** this is the single most safety-critical invariant in the whole synchronization design — releasing the Proxy on "signal delivered" instead of "task completed" would silently break the entire lockstep guarantee. The dedicated test file proves this was verified, not assumed.

**Issue → CAMUNDA REFUSING TO DEPLOY GENERATED BPMNS (ENGINE-09005)**
- **Fix in code:** `camunda.bpm.generic-properties.properties.enforceHistoryTimeToLive=false`
- **Evidence:** commit `30d8156`: *"RedCollarTP now disables Camunda's enforced historyTimeToLive (ENGINE-09005) — ... every generated platform was refusing to deploy without it."*
- **Why it matters:** stated plainly as a hard blocker — every generated platform failed to deploy at all until this was added. This is unambiguous "it didn't work, then I fixed it," not preemptive configuration.

**Issue → GENERATED SPRING BEAN NAME COLLISION BETWEEN PROXY AND TWIN ACTIVITIES SHARING AN ID**
- **Fix in code:** twin-side delegate beans get a `Twin`-suffixed name
- **Evidence:** commit `89b397a`: *"Fix Proxy/Twin Spring bean-name collision for delegate-expression activities that share an activity id across an authored twin and its proxy (ConflictingBeanDefinitionException at startup)."* Regression tests added at both the generator and authored-twin entry point.
- **Why it matters:** `ConflictingBeanDefinitionException` is a hard Spring Boot startup failure — the generated app would not even start. This confirms it actually happened during testing, was diagnosed, and got a regression test to prevent recurrence.

**Issue → BUILD FAILURE MISREPORTED AS A GENERIC LAUNCH TIMEOUT**
- **Fix in code:** `mvn clean install -DskipTests` run before `mvn spring-boot:run` for wrapper-less templates
- **Evidence:** commit `30d8156`: *"so a build failure surfaces as its own clear error with its own build.log instead of the generic 'never started listening' timeout."*
- **Why it matters:** direct evidence that before this fix, a broken generated project produced an unhelpful, misleading timeout error rather than the actual compile error — a real debugging-experience problem that got fixed.

**Issue → TWIN BPMN DIAGRAM ELEMENTS GETTING RANDOM IDS ON EACH GENERATION (spurious redeployment)**
- **Fix in code:** derive each DI element's id from the stable twin element id it depicts
- **Evidence:** commit `30d8156`: *"defeated enableDuplicateFiltering (relaunching an unchanged model kept deploying a spurious new Twin version)."*
- **Why it matters:** without this, every relaunch of an unchanged model created a new Camunda process definition version — polluting the deployment history and breaking any comparison across launches.

## Strongest Evidence

1. **`4ffb6d8` commit message** — explicitly states "Two race conditions found and fixed during concurrency/rework-loop hardening," naming both by mechanism, and the diff shows `everDelivered`/`partnerArrivalTicks` being introduced with comments explaining exactly what failure mode they close.
2. **`LockstepTimingInvariantTest.java`** — a dedicated 278-line test (added in the same session as the lockstep fix) that deliberately blocks a Twin delegate mid-execution with a `CountDownLatch` and asserts the Proxy cannot advance — this is a test written specifically to catch a timing violation, not a generic unit test.
3. **The `application.properties` retry comment in `RedCollarTP`** — states in its own words that a previous fast-failure mode was misdiagnosed by `SpringBootProjectLauncher.awaitReady` as a broken project, and the retry config was added specifically to correct that misdiagnosis.
4. **`89b397a` commit** — a `ConflictingBeanDefinitionException` at generated-app startup, fixed with a naming scheme change, with new regression tests added at two separate entry points to prevent recurrence.
5. **`RedCollarTargetPlatformSyncEndToEndTest`** (referenced in `30d8156`'s own verification note) — the commit explicitly states this was "verified against the real professor-supplied RedCollar BPMNs... through the real RedCollarTP template end to end," i.e., this proof was run against the actual broker and actual generated project, not simulated.

## What I Can Say to Joanna

"Getting Proxy/Twin synchronization working over RabbitMQ took a few real rounds of debugging, and the git history documents them directly. Two genuine race conditions came up: a Twin that started slightly after its Proxy had already passed a shared signal would wait forever with nothing to release it, and a signal that only exists in one side's BPMN — like `orderVerifySignal` in the real Manuf file — had a registered partner that would structurally never co-wait on it, so that also hung indefinitely. Both got fixed with tracking state in `SignalBroadcaster` — an `everDelivered` set and a bounded retry counter — so either case now falls back to direct delivery instead of hanging. Separately, the generated app initially failed to even deploy because Camunda enforces a history-retention setting our generated BPMNs didn't carry, and there was a Spring bean-naming collision when the Proxy and Twin shared an activity id, which threw a hard startup exception until the Twin-side beans got their own distinct names. There's also a dedicated test, `LockstepTimingInvariantTest`, written specifically to prove the Proxy can't advance until the Twin's gated task has actually finished executing — not just been signaled — since that distinction is the whole point of the synchronization guarantee. So the debugging was real, it's documented in the commit history, and each fix has a comment or test tied to the specific failure it addresses."
